first_reason: 'visible' only means it can be seen. 'Conspicuous' means it stands out. 'Not visible' would wrongly become 'not conspicuous'.
reason: 'Veins visible' means clearly visible. The accepted rules for evident, obvious, well-defined and well-marked all map to PATO:0000463 conspicuous. Negated forms ('not visible', 'invisible', 'scarcely visible') have their own rules to inconspicuous (R0067, R0173, R0136), so the negation worry does not arise.

first_reason: 'Confluent' means running together or merging (veins, glands, spots). It does not mean fused organs (connate).
reason: For like parts that run together into one (sori, segments, lobes, appendages), FLOPO connate (like parts united by tissue fusion) fits, as with the accepted 'coalescent' rule. Confluent veins (anastomosing), spots and glands (colour or surface pattern) are not fusion of organs, so the rule should apply only to organ-type parts.

first_reason: 'Delicate' in floras usually means slender or fine. It does not mean fragile, and no better target exists.
reason: In floras 'delicate' means thin, slender, fine, tender or easily damaged, depending on the part. PATO fragile is a disposition to break and covers only one of these readings. No single existing class fits, so the word should stay unmapped.

first_reason: 'Septate' means divided by septa (partitions). 'Split' means cleft, which is a different meaning.
reason: PATO:0001786 split (divided into parts) has 'septate' as an explicit NARROW synonym in ont/quality.obo. PO:0000030 septum (used by rule R0445) only covers partitions of cavities formed by fused organs, so it would not fit septate hairs. Split is the existing class that covers all the uses.

first_reason: 'Rolled' (margins revolute or involute, leaves convolute) is a specific rolling. 'Curled' is a different shape.
reason: In PATO, involute (0001962), revolute (0001963) and convolute (0001966) are all subclasses of curled (0000405). Bare 'rolled' does not give the direction, so the parent class is the correct, safe mapping.

first_reason: 'Rooting' means rooting at the nodes of stems, so the shoot-borne root only fits on these parts. Elsewhere it is ambiguous.
reason: 'Rooting' (at the nodes, at the tips) means roots arising from the shoot system, which is PO:0000042 shoot-borne root. That holds for stems, stolons, nodes and also fronds and leaf tips (walking ferns). It should not apply when the bearer is a root.

first_reason: 'Apparent' means visible or evident. It does not mean conspicuous, as with 'visible' in R0001.
reason: 'Veins apparent' means clearly visible, the same reading as 'evident' (C323). The opposite, 'not apparent', is already mapped to inconspicuous (R0526), so the pair stays consistent.

first_reason: 'Mat' is dull only in French or as 'matt'. In English, 'mat' is a noun for a mat-forming habit. Limit it to surfaces.
reason: French 'mat' (English 'matt') means not shiny, which is FLOPO:0991106 dull, but the English noun 'mat' means mat-forming (FLOPO:0991010). Limiting the rule to surface-bearing parts avoids catching the noun on a whole plant.

first_reason: 'Gregarious' means growing in groups. It describes plants, not a part. 'Aggregated' (clustered) is close but not the same, so a rule is risky.
reason: When said of plants, 'gregarious' means growing in groups, which fits PATO aggregated (clumped, clustered). 'Gregarious flowering' (synchronised mass flowering) is a different meaning, so the rule should apply only to whole-plant bearers.

first_reason: Bicolored means exactly two colours. 'Multi-colored' loses the 'two'. Use it only if there is no bicolored class.
reason: PATO multi-colored is defined as 'two or more hues', so bicolored is a correct (if broader) mapping and no bicolored class exists. This matches the accepted rule R0552 'bicoloured'. For leaves with two differently coloured faces, FLOPO discolorous is more exact.

first_reason: Heteromorphic means two or more different forms. Dimorphic means exactly two. Use polymorphic or a rule with a constraint, not dimorphic.
reason: Heteromorphic means occurring in different forms, not necessarily two. The accepted rule R0102 maps 'polymorphic' to PATO variant shape, with FLOPO dimorphic as the narrower two-form case. Mapping to dimorphic would claim exactly two forms where the text does not say so.

first_reason: Epigeal describes germination with cotyledons raised above ground. It is not the same as 'aerial' (borne in the air).
reason: Epigeal stems, stolons and cotyledons are above the ground, which is FLOPO aerial; the accepted 'epigeous' rule (R0569) gives the same reading. 'Germination epigeal' with a seed or seedling as bearer is a germination type, not a position, so it must be excluded.

first_reason: Shaggy means long, soft, tangled hairs. Villous means long, soft, unmatted hairs. They are similar but the 'tangled' part is lost.
reason: FLOPO:0991051 villous is defined as 'bearing long, soft, shaggy hairs', so shaggy is covered by the definition itself. 'Shaggy bark' (exfoliating) is the only misfit and is rare among the examples.

first_reason: Ample means large or spacious. It is fine for broad organs, but 'increased size' is not clearly meant for every part.
reason: 'Ample' panicles, sheaths and blades are large, which is PATO increased size (relatively high size; synonyms big, enlarged). The examples include panicles and sheaths, so the organ list proposed by the first check is too narrow.

first_reason: Cracked can describe bark or soil surface cracks, not only fissures. For bark it fits, for other parts it is unclear.
reason: 'Cracked' is already a listed synonym of FLOPO:0991022 fissured, whose definition covers bark, other surfaces and axes. It matches the accepted rules for 'cracking' (R0366) and 'rimose' (R0619).

first_reason: Widening is a process. 'Dilated' means already widened. Map it only with a bearer constraint, if at all.
reason: 'Widening distally' describes a part that becomes wider along its length, which is the shape PATO dilated describes, not a process. It matches the accepted rules 'expanding' (R0508), 'ampliate' (R0225) and 'expanded' (C181).

first_reason: Corrugate means folded in ridges and furrows. Rugose means wrinkled. They are close but not the same.
reason: Corrugate surfaces are thrown into wrinkles or folds, which is PATO rugose. The accepted rules 'corrugated' (R0097), 'puckered' (R0262) and 'rugulate' (R0660) all use the same class.

first_reason: Not visible means hidden or absent from view, not small. 'Inconspicuous' means hard to notice, which is weaker.
reason: 'Veins not visible' means not clearly visible. The accepted rules for invisible, hardly visible, barely visible, imperceptible, obscure and indistinct all map to PATO:0000464 inconspicuous. Relational uses ('not visible through the utricle') go to pattern 09.

first_reason: Buff is a pale yellowish brown, not orange yellow.
reason: config/botanical_colour_synonyms.tsv (ISCC-NBS based) already maps buff and all its compounds (pale buff, grayish buff and others) to PATO:0104054 orange yellow. Changing only this rule would make the colour mapping inconsistent. PATO beige could be considered if the colour table itself is revised.

first_reason: Tridentate means three-toothed. Tricuspidate means three-pointed. They are similar but the teeth and cusps differ.
reason: PATO:0002256 tricuspidate (having three cusps) is the existing term for an apex with three teeth or points; there is no tridentate class. Using a count of three teeth (pattern 03) is the only other option, and a rule to an existing term is preferred.

first_reason: Produced means extended or drawn out (for example, a leaf produced into a tip). Excurrent means the axis runs through the apex. Not the same.
reason: 'Connective produced beyond the thecae' and 'rachilla produced' fit FLOPO excurrent (extending beyond the apex of the structure it runs through). 'Leaf produced into a tip' or 'base produced into a spur' do not fit, so the rule should apply only to axial parts that run through a structure.

first_reason: Ramiflorous means flowers on branches. Cauliflorous means flowers on the trunk. They are different.
reason: The definition of FLOPO:0991175 cauliflorous covers flowers arising 'from the trunk or from older, leafless woody branches', so ramiflory falls inside it.

first_reason: Narrowly rounded is a kind of rounded apex, not blunt. Blunt is a different shape.
reason: PATO:0001950 blunt is defined as 'terminating gradually in a rounded end', which describes a narrowly rounded apex. Plain 'rounded' maps to obtuse, but 'narrowly' points to the gradual rounded tip that blunt describes.

first_reason: The word 'sparsely' (hair density) is lost. Use pubescent with a density value or leave it unmapped.
reason: This is pubescent plus a degree word. The playbook drops degree modifiers and keeps them as a cue in the record (as with 'longitudinally fissured'), and there is no 'sparsely pubescent' class.

first_reason: Apical means at the tip. For leaf and fruit parts it can mean the apex region, not the terminal position.
reason: PATO terminal means located at an end. Apical pores, anthers, inflorescences and apical hairs on a leaf are all at the end of the part that bears them. 'Apical or subapical' pairs with PATO subterminal. The first check's restriction would exclude correct uses such as anther pores.

first_reason: As an adjective, 'aggregate' fits clustered parts. It also names a fruit type (aggregate fruit), so the meaning changes by part.
reason: Aggregate spikes and pseudobulbs are clustered, which is PATO aggregated. 'Aggregate fruit' names a part (PO:0025628 aggregate fruit) and should change the bearer, not become a quality, so fruit must be excluded.

first_reason: Erect-spreading means erect and spreading together. Semi erect is a different, partly upright state.
reason: Erect-spreading means directed obliquely upward, between erect and spreading. The accepted rule R0499 maps the same word 'erect-patent' to PATO ascending, which is defined as directed upward at an oblique angle. Semi erect is a kind of erect and is vaguer.

first_reason: 'Rooted' means bearing roots. Shoot-borne roots fit stems at nodes. It should not apply to a plant or a root.
reason: Stems, stolons and nodes that are rooted bear shoot-borne roots (PO:0000042). For a whole plant ('deeply rooted'), 'rooted' refers to the main root system, not shoot-borne roots, and for a root bearer it makes no sense.

first_reason: Echinulate means with small spines or prickles. 'Spiny' loses the small size.
reason: Echinulate means minutely echinate, and echinate is already mapped to PATO:0001365 spiny (C306). No diminutive class exists, so the broader existing term is preferred over a new one.

first_reason: Sclerified means thickened by sclerenchyma. Hard is only the result. It also changes the tissue meaning.
reason: Sclerified endocarps, perigone segments and roots are hardened by thick-walled cells. The accepted rules for indurate (C305), sclerotic (R0546), horny and corneous all map to PATO:0000386 hard.

first_reason: Chaffy means covered in chaff-like scales or paleae. Scarious means thin and dry. They are different.
reason: On bracts, scales, stipules and glume-like parts, chaffy means thin, dry and membranous, which is FLOPO scarious. 'Receptacle chaffy' means paleae are present, which is flower bract (PO_0009034, synonym chaff) present, so the receptacle must be excluded and given its own rule.

first_reason: Corrugated means folded in ridges and furrows. Rugose means wrinkled. They are close but not the same.
reason: Corrugated seeds, fruits, bark and blades have a surface thrown into many wrinkles or folds, which is PATO:0001359 rugose. The accepted rule R0066 already maps 'corrugate' to rugose; plicate and furrowed are narrower or different.

first_reason: Curved-ascending means curved and then ascending. Ascending alone loses the curve.
reason: PATO:0104355 ascending is 'directed gradually upward at an oblique angle', which is what a curved-ascending stem or pedicel does. The curve is part of the botanical sense of ascending, not a second value.

first_reason: Reclining means leaning or resting on a support, not decumbent (lying on the ground with tips turned up).
reason: Reclining is ambiguous in floras: leaning on a support (semi-scandent), lying down, or bent backwards. It is not reliably decumbent (lying on the ground with rising tips). PATO:0001965 reclinate is a curled quality and does not fit either.

first_reason: Umbelliform describes inflorescence form. A tree crown or a fruit can also be umbrella-shaped, and that is a different meaning.
reason: FLOPO umbelliform is defined only for inflorescences with flowers arising from about one point. An umbrella-shaped crown, stigma or fruit is a different, flat-topped spreading shape.

first_reason: Polymorphic means variable in form. PATO variant shape means a shape that differs from the normal one. The rule loses the 'varies between forms' meaning, so it is better not mapped.
reason: 'Polymorphic' is mostly said of species or populations (a taxonomic remark), or of variation in colour, hairiness or size, not only shape. Mapping it to PATO variant shape on the bearer would make false phenotypes. The dimorphic and heterophylly cases need their own terms.

first_reason: Baccate means berry-like, so fleshy fits fruit. It does not fit other parts.
reason: Baccate means berry-like, so fleshy is right for fruits and for fleshy cones or seeds (Juniperus, Taxus). On other parts the word does not occur in that sense.

first_reason: Included means not protruding, which is the opposite of exserted, so it applies to stamens, styles and similar parts. 'Enclosed' on other parts, such as a seed in a fruit, only describes containment.
reason: FLOPO included means not projecting beyond the structure that encloses it, and it is not limited to stamens and styles. Its bearer list already includes fruit, sepal and ovary parts. 'Stamens enclosed', 'nut enclosed in the cupule' and 'fruit enclosed by the accrescent calyx' are all this quality. The enclosing part is missing in both words alike.

first_reason: Metallic means a metal-like sheen, often with colour such as metallic blue. Glistening loses the metal-like part.
reason: A metallic sheen or lustre is a kind of high reflectivity, so it falls under PATO:0001373 glistening. The metal-like detail is lost, but the parent is correct, as with arcuate to curved. A colour word with it ('metallic blue') is mapped separately. Iridescent needs a colour change with viewing angle.

first_reason: Paleaceous means chaffy or bearing paleae (scales). Scarious means thin, dry and membranous. They overlap but are not the same, so the rule loses the 'bearing chaff scales' meaning.
reason: Paleaceous of pappus elements, bracts and scales means chaffy, which is scarious. 'Receptacle paleaceous' (Asteraceae) means the receptacle bears paleae, which is flower bract (PO_0009034) present, so the receptacle must be excluded.

first_reason: Flanged means having a flange or rim. A wing is a broader, flatter outgrowth, so the rule loses the 'rim' meaning.
reason: A flange is a thin, flattened rim projecting from the body (spore equator, fruit, stipule margin). That fits PATO:0104354 winged ('thin, flattened extensions that project from its main body'). A flange is a narrow wing, not a different quality.

first_reason: PO uses awn for grass spikelet parts. A bristle-tipped leaf or phyllary has a bristle or mucro, not an awn.
reason: PO:0025349 awn is defined as an appendage of a glume, lemma or palea. A bristle-tipped leaf, tooth or phyllary has a bristle point, which is better covered by FLOPO hair-pointed (FLOPO:0991249) or mucronate (FLOPO:0991054), not by awn present.

first_target: PATO_0001325 radial symmetry (or PATO_0001328 actinomorphic, for flowers)
first_reason: In descriptions, radial usually means radial symmetry. Radiating means spreading out from a centre, which is a different thing.
reason: 'Radial' is ambiguous: radial symmetry of flowers, radial walls and sections, radially arranged ribs or rays. Radiating fits only the last. The flower sense already has R0607 (radially symmetric to actinomorphic); a flower-only rule for 'radial' to PATO:0001328 actinomorphic can be added separately.

first_reason: Pithy means containing pith in stems. For fruit, 'pithy' means a spongy flesh, which is not the pith.
reason: On stems and axes, pithy means containing pith (PO:0006109). On fruit it means spongy flesh, which is not pith.

first_reason: 'Panicled' says the flowers or inflorescence are arranged as a panicle. A rule that only says a panicle is present loses that.
reason: 'Flowers panicled' or 'inflorescence panicled' says the flowers are borne in a panicle, so panicle inflorescence (PO:0030123) present is the right reading. This matches how 'aristate' is mapped to awn present (C207). When the adjective qualifies another named inflorescence type, FLOPO panicle-like (FLOPO:0991198) is the alternative.

first_reason: Knobbed means bearing knobs, which is knobbled. Head-shaped (capitate) is a different word.
reason: In floras, 'knobbed' styles, stigmas, hairs and connectives end in a knob, which is the FLOPO head-shaped definition ('abruptly enlarged at its tip into a rounded head'). A surface bearing many knobs is 'knobby/knobbly' (PATO:0002427 knobbled), a different word.

first_reason: 'Crisp' can mean crisped (a curled margin) on leaves and petals. On other parts it can mean a brittle texture.
reason: FLOPO crisped is a margin quality, and 'crisp' means crisped on leaf and perianth parts. On fruits, stems and other parts 'crisp' means a brittle texture, and on hairs it means curly.

first_reason: Sarmentose means bearing long, slender, trailing or whip-like shoots. That is not the same as climbing, and it loses the runner or trailing sense.
reason: The rule is already limited to plant, stem and habit. In the tropical floras (French 'sarmenteux'), a sarmentose shrub is a scrambling, half-climbing one. FLOPO climbing is defined to include leaning on a support. The runner (stolon) sense is rare in these descriptions.

first_reason: Well-defined means distinct or sharply delimited, not conspicuous. The two can differ.
reason: Well-defined usually means sharply delimited or distinct from the neighbouring part (well-defined petiole, keel, border), not clearly visible. There is no PATO or FLOPO term for 'distinct', and PATO:0005006 differentiated from needs the second part.

first_reason: Embedded means sunk in or enclosed by another tissue, such as seeds in pulp or glands in the surface. That is a position, not the sunken shape of a surface.
reason: Glands, stomata and sori that are embedded in the surface are below its level, which is PATO:0002416 sunken. 'Seeds embedded in pulp' describes containment, and sunken would be wrong there.

first_reason: Invisible means cannot be seen at all. Inconspicuous only means hard to see, so the rule loses the absolute sense.
reason: 'Veins invisible' or 'nerves invisible beneath' is the extreme of not being clearly visible, which falls under PATO:0000464 inconspicuous. It does not say the part is absent, so the broader correct term is the safe mapping.

first_reason: Gland-like means resembling a gland, but it is not a gland. Glandular means bearing glands.
reason: Gland-like means resembling a gland (gland-like teeth, appendages), not bearing glands or being glandular tissue. Mapping it to PATO:0002117 glandular would claim glands are present.

first_reason: Veiny means conspicuously veined. The rule says only that veins are present and loses the conspicuousness. The target is also the vascular bundle, not the leaf vein.
reason: Veiny means conspicuously veined, which is a visibility statement, not presence. The target PO:0005020 is the vascular bundle, not leaf lamina vein (PO:0020138). The right form is vein + conspicuous (a pattern with a part), not a single-word rule.

first_reason: 'Level' is vague. It can mean even or flat, or level with a surface, and flush is not the general sense.
reason: 'Level' is vague (flat, even, 'at the level of', 'level with' X). PATO flush needs a second surface, which the word alone does not give.

first_reason: Laminate is ambiguous. It can mean layered or flattened, so it does not reliably mean that a lamina is present.
reason: Laminate means either having a blade or layered (bark, testa). It does not reliably mean that a lamina is present.

first_reason: Tetrahedral means a four-faced solid with triangular faces. Pyramidal loses the four-face and triangular-face detail.
reason: A tetrahedron is a triangular pyramid, so tetrahedral is a narrower case of PATO:0002336 pyramidal. Mapping to the broader correct class is acceptable, as with arcuate to curved.

first_reason: Poorly defined usually describes indistinct margins or veins. It does not mean low visibility (inconspicuous). Reject, or map it to an 'indistinct' term if one exists.
reason: Poorly defined margins, zones or veins are indistinctly delimited, which is not the same as low visibility. There is no 'indistinct' term. This matches the drop of 'well-defined' (R0160).

first_reason: Obtusely pointed means an obtuse apex (angle over 90°). It is not subacute, which is nearly acute.
reason: An obtusely pointed apex narrows to a blunt point, which is the same reading as 'blunt-pointed', already mapped to PATO obtuse (R1816). It is not subacute (nearly acute).

first_reason: Stigmatic means 'of the stigma' (stigmatic surface, lobes, hairs). It does not say a stigma is present, so entity_presence is wrong. Reject the rule.
reason: Stigmatic means 'of the stigma' (stigmatic surface, lobes, branches). It names part of the stigma, so it belongs with the bearer, and it does not state that a stigma is present.

first_reason: Bicolorous means two colours on the same part. Discolorous means the two surfaces differ in colour. Reject, or map to a two-coloured term.
reason: Bicolorous means a part has two colours (for example petals white with a pink base). PATO multi-colored (synonym variegated) is the correct broader term. FLOPO discolorous is about compared surfaces, typically the two leaf faces, differing in colour.

first_reason: Anisophyllous means leaves of different size or shape on one plant. Unequal (size of a set) loses the shape part and the leaf-set meaning.
reason: In flora usage, anisophylly almost always means the leaves of a pair or node differ in size. That is exactly FLOPO unequal (FLOPO:0991101), a size quality of a set of like parts. It says nothing about how many forms there are, so it adds nothing false. The rule already moves whole-plant statements to the leaves. Differences in shape are rare and stay in the source words.

first_reason: Monadelphous means filaments united into one bundle. The generic connate loses 'one group', and diadelphous already has its own class under connate. Use a monadelphous class.
reason: Monadelphous filaments are fused with one another, so connate (FLOPO:0991067) is true. The rule only applies to stamens, filaments and androecium. Mapping to the parent class loses 'one bundle' but asserts nothing wrong, the same as rolled → curled. Monadelphous (99 statements) is a good candidate for a later class next to diadelphous (FLOPO:0991259). Until then the parent is the right fallback.

first_reason: Crisped is an edge shape. Curly also describes hairs, stems, tendrils and twigs, where an edge shape is wrong.
reason: Curly hairs ('poils frisés') are crisped hairs in standard glossary use. FLOPO crisped already lists trichome bearers, so the first check's list wrongly leaves out the main use. Curly stems, tendrils and twigs mean bent or coiled axes, not a crisped edge, so leave them out. Crisped's edge-shape parent (PATO:0002267) should be widened for hairs, as the rule's own note says.

first_reason: Well defined usually describes distinct margins or veins, not conspicuousness. Reject, or map to a 'distinct' term.
reason: 'Well defined' means clearly visible and marked off. That matches how the earlier review mapped 'distinct' to conspicuous (C176), and C176 was limited to veins and similar features. Limiting this rule the same way avoids cases where 'well defined' means separate or free, which belongs to C177.

first_reason: Not prolonged means not extended or elongated. It is not the same as not excurrent, which refers to extending beyond the apex. Reject.
reason: Most cases are 'connective not prolonged above the thecae' or a midrib or rachis not continued beyond the apex. That is exactly not excurrent (FLOPO:0991162: extending beyond the apex of the structure it runs through). On other parts (corolla tube, style, lobes), 'not prolonged' means not elongated, and excurrent is wrong there.

first_reason: Hollowed can mean concave on flat parts. On stems or fruits it means hollow (an internal cavity), and concave is wrong there.
reason: 'Hollowed abaxially' or 'deeply hollowed' on flat or surface parts means curving inward: PATO concave. On trunks, stems or fruits, 'hollowed' means an inner cavity, which is PATO hollow (PATO:0002078). Those parts are left out.

first_reason: Gamopetalous means the petals are united. Connate is only right when the bearer is the corolla, petals or flower, and wrong for other parts.
reason: Gamopetalous only ever describes the corolla (its petals fused to one another), so the word cannot mean anything else. Connate (FLOPO:0991067) is right, as for 'united' (C171). A bearer limit adds nothing. The rule already puts the corolla's petals as the bearer.

first_reason: Lacunose means a surface with irregular pits or gaps, or a tissue with air spaces. It does not mean that an anatomical space is present as an entity. The right class is a surface-pitted quality, not an entity presence.
reason: On leaves, midribs and stems, 'lacunose' means having lacunae (air spaces). PO plant anatomical space lists lacuna as an exact synonym, so a presence statement fits. A lacunose receptacle, endocarp or seed is pitted, which is foveate (C179), so surface parts are left out.

first_reason: Torn describes an irregularly cut margin on laminar parts. On other parts it can mean damage.
reason: Lacerate (FLOPO:0991115) is a margin cut irregularly as if torn, which fits flat parts and sheaths. On fruit valves or bark, or for specimen damage ('leaves often torn'), 'torn' means splitting or damage, not a margin shape.

first_reason: Not distinct is ambiguous. For veins or glands it means indistinct, but for stamens or lobes it means united. It should not be mapped to inconspicuous.
reason: This follows the earlier split of 'distinct'. On veins and similar parts it means clearly visible (C176), so 'not distinct' there is inconspicuous, like 'indistinct' (C175). On stamens, petals, styles and lobes, 'distinct' means free (C177), so 'not distinct' would mean connate. Those parts must not get inconspicuous.

first_reason: Brochidodromous is a venation term. Looping elsewhere, such as stems or tendrils, means something different.
reason: Secondary veins looping before the margin are brochidodromous venation (PATO:0001970). Looping stems, branches or tendrils mean a curved axis, not venation.

first_reason: Irregularly divided is not just split. It loses the irregularity and the sense of leaf division into lobes or segments. Reject, or use a divided or lobed class.
reason: Divided means split into parts, and PATO split is the parent of laciniate, pedate and parted. 'Irregularly' describes manner, not a separate quality, and the earlier reviews treat such words as dropped detail. Mapping to the parent is true. A narrower class like laciniate would add details the text does not give.

first_reason: Not rooting means the stem does not root at its nodes, which maps to shoot-borne root absent. For other parts it does not mean that.
reason: This is the negation of R0032 'rooting' → shoot-borne root present (synonym adventitious root), which has no bearer limit. 'Not rooting' is only said of stems, stolons, nodes, branches or whole plants, and roots from any shoot part count as shoot-borne. A limit would make it inconsistent with R0032.

first_reason: Narrowed means made narrow or constricted, which is not the same as tapered. Not narrowed is not not tapered.
reason: 'Narrowed (to the base or apex)' is mapped to PATO tapered by the accepted rule C172 (2394 statements). Its negation is therefore not tapered. The first check's idea that 'narrowed' means constricted is not how floras use it. Constricted cases use 'constricted' or 'abruptly narrowed' (FLOPO:0991316).

first_reason: Not expanded usually means unopened or unfolded, as in a bud, corolla or leaf. It does not mean not dilated, which is a widening.
reason: C181 maps 'expanded' to dilated only for the widened-base sense (filament base, style apex), so 'not expanded' is not dilated there. On buds, leaves, corollas and flowers, 'not expanded' means not yet unfolded or opened, a stage of development. Dilated is wrong for those parts.

first_reason: parenchymatous says a given part is made of parenchyma. The rule drops that part and only asserts that parenchyma exists. Better as a tissue-composition annotation, or leave it unmapped.
reason: For tissues and organs, 'parenchymatous' means made of parenchyma. Parenchyma present (PO synonym 'portion of parenchymatous tissue') is a weaker but true statement. In bryology, 'cells parenchymatous' describes cell shape (short and blunt-ended rather than elongate and pointed), and presence is wrong there. So cells are left out.

first_reason: ligulate means strap-shaped for corollas and florets. In grasses and ferns it means having a ligule, so the negation would mean no ligule there.
reason: This negates C189 (ligulate = strap-shaped), which was set for corollas, petals and sepals. In grasses, sedges and some ferns, 'ligulate' means having a ligule (PO_0020105). For leaves, sheaths, stipules and lemmas, 'not ligulate' means ligule absent, not 'not strap-shaped', so lemma is left out too.

first_reason: heterophyllous means leaves of different forms, possibly more than two. Dimorphic fixes the number at two.
reason: Heterophylly means leaves of different forms on one plant, and there can be more than two. FLOPO dimorphic (FLOPO:0991092) states exactly two forms, which adds a claim the text does not make. No existing parent class means 'of several forms', so this needs a new class (a parent of dimorphic and sibling of monomorphic) rather than a rule.

first_reason: incurving means curving inward; curved loses the direction
reason: Incurving is curving gradually inward. PATO curved is a true parent class, as already accepted for arcuate (C185). Inflexed (FLOPO:0991145) is an abrupt bend and involute is a rolled margin, so neither fits. Losing the direction is acceptable until an 'incurved' class exists.

first_reason: stipe-like means looking like a stalk, as a narrowed base does. Stipitate means borne on a stalk. No better target is known.
reason: In 'stipe-like base' or 'stipe-like internode', the bearer is the stalk-like part itself. Stipitate (FLOPO:0991065, borne on a stalk) would wrongly say that part is carried on a stalk. FLOPO deals with resemblance words through 'X-like' shape classes (petiole-like FLOPO:0991298, stolon-like). Stipe-like would need its own class.

first_reason: rim-like means like a low raised edge (a calyx or cupule rim), not necessarily a ring shape. Better rejected.
reason: A rim-like disc or calyx is a low ring round the receptacle or ovary. An annular disc is a standard phrase, and PATO ring shaped has annular as an exact synonym. On other parts, 'rim-like' means a raised edge or margin, not a ring.

first_reason: well-spaced means evenly or adequately spaced. Distant means widely separated.
reason: Well-spaced flowers, lobes or veins are clearly and fairly widely separated, which matches FLOPO distant (widely separated from the nearest structures of its kind). 'Well-spaced' does not say the spacing is even, so evenly spaced (FLOPO:0991365) would add a claim.

first_reason: narrow-elliptic means narrowly elliptic; elliptic loses the narrowness (the length-to-width ratio)
reason: 'Narrowly' is a degree word. The earlier review accepted the same treatment for 'narrowly oval' and 'narrowly cylindric' (R0271, R0264). The shape is PATO elliptic, and any stated length-to-width ratio goes to pattern 11.

first_reason: loses the appressed (lying flat) part of the hair description
reason: The surface is canescent (FLOPO:0991079). 'Appressed' describes the hairs, not the surface, and can be added as appressed (FLOPO:0991064) on the trichomes. The rule asserts nothing wrong and keeps the main content.

first_reason: ungulate means hoof-shaped; clawed (unguiculate) is a different word. Better rejected.
reason: In these floras, 'ungulate' is a misspelling of unguiculate ('base long ungulate'; French 'onguiculés'), so clawed (FLOPO:0991169, synonym unguiculate) is right for perianth parts and bracts. Limiting it to those parts keeps out the real meaning, 'hoof-shaped', on other parts.

first_reason: 'Obtusely' says the angle is wide. Plain 'angular' drops that.
reason: Stems, achenes and fruits with blunt angles are angular (PATO:0001977). 'Obtusely' is the degree of the angle, which PATO does not split, so this is the same degree-word treatment as narrow-elliptic.

first_reason: The target is a petal spur. Spurs can also be on sepals or the calyx, so the rule fits only petal-like parts.
reason: PO has petal spur (PO_0025511) and corolla spur, but no general spur class. Spurless sepals, calyx, anthers or whole flowers (where a sepal spur may be meant, as in Tropaeolum or Delphinium) cannot be expressed as 'petal spur absent'.

first_reason: PO costa is the midrib of a moss phyllid. In flowering plants and ferns, ecostate means no midrib or ribs, so the target does not fit. No better term was found.
reason: 'Ecostate' is mainly a moss term (69 statements in 6 floras, nearly all moss leaves). PO costa (PO_0030072) is the non-vascular leaf midrib and has phyllid costa and midrib as synonyms, so the target fits the main use. The first check's angiosperm and fern sense is rare for this word.

first_reason: The value term fissured is for bark or axes. 'Cracking' can also mean a fruit or capsule splitting open.
reason: Fissured (FLOPO:0991022) is defined for bark and axes and has cracked as a related synonym. Cracking capsules or fruits are splitting open, which belongs to dehiscent (FLOPO:0991149) and its children, not fissured.

first_reason: 'Indument' is a noun that names the part, not a statement that it is present. It is already a bearer word (FLOPO_0986003). As a quality it would assert presence wrongly in cases like 'indument absent'.
reason: When 'indument' appears in the quality field ('leaves with indument', 'indument of stellate hairs'), the statement asserts the covering is there, so indumentum present (FLOPO:0986003) is right. 'Indument absent' puts 'indument' in the bearer field and 'absent' in the quality field, so this rule cannot fire there. The first check's worry does not apply.

first_reason: Underdeveloped is about incomplete development (rudimentary, hypoplastic), not only a smaller size.
reason: 'Underdeveloped' can mean reduced or rudimentary, or simply not yet developed (young). 'Decreased size' loses that meaning. PATO vestigial (a remnant structure) and hypoplastic (fewer cells) do not fit either. Too ambiguous for one class.

first_reason: Weeping means hanging down for branches and crowns. It can also mean exuding, as with resin or sap from bark.
reason: PATO drooping (bending or hanging downwards) is right for weeping branches, crowns and habit. On bark or wounds, 'weeping' means exuding sap or resin.

first_reason: A denuded stem can be bare of leaves, but it can also be stripped of hairs, bark or scales. It does not always mean leaf absent.
reason: On a stem, 'denuded' can mean stripped of leaves, hairs, scales or bark. Leaf absent is only one of these, and the rule would also wrongly say an older stem section never had leaves.

first_reason: 'Irregularly' contradicts the exact rectangular shape, so the target loses the irregularity.
reason: 'Irregularly' contradicts the exact right-angled outline of PATO rectangular, so the mapping would state a precise shape the text denies.

first_reason: Withering is a process of drying up, often while the part stays on (marcescent). It does not mean a shriveled shape.
reason: 'Withering' describes a process, often of persistent parts ('withering and persistent'). PATO shriveled is a resulting state, and marcescent (FLOPO:0991181) also needs persistence. The word is not a reliable cue for either.

first_reason: Epaleate means without paleae (chaff scales), as on a composite receptacle. For grasses, a palea is a different part.
reason: On a composite receptacle, paleae are chaff bracts, and PO flower bract has 'chaff' as a synonym, so 'flower bract absent' fits there. A grass palea is a different structure.

first_reason: The target is a fruit operculum. Operculate also describes seeds, flowers or buds, and moss capsules.
reason: PO fruit operculum (fruit lid) is right only on fruits. Operculate buds or calyces (e.g. Eucalyptus) and seeds have other lids.

first_reason: Contracted means narrowed or shortened overall, as in an inflorescence. Constricted means pinched at a point. They are different.
reason: 'Contracted' (shortened or crowded overall, as in a panicle) is not 'constricted' (narrowed at one point). The negation maps to the wrong quality.

first_reason: 'Sparsely' limits the amount of leaves, and 'leafy' loses it. It would assert a well-leaved part.
reason: FLOPO:0991012 leafy means bearing well-developed foliage. 'Sparsely leafy' says nearly the opposite, so the mapping would mislead.

first_reason: The target 'floating' means resting on the water surface. Free-floating also means not attached to the ground, and it can mean submerged. The class's own note says free-floating plants must be kept apart from floating organs.
reason: FLOPO:0991045 floating means resting on the water surface, and its own note asks to keep free-floating plants apart. 'Free-floating' (not attached to the ground, possibly submerged) needs its own class or a pattern.

first_reason: Apiculate is a short, sharp, flexible tip. Mucronulate is a small stiff mucro. They are close but not the same, and the extra word 'short' is lost.
reason: Apiculate (a short, sharp, flexible point) is not mucronulate (FLOPO:0991055, a minute mucro, under mucronate). FLOPO has no apiculate value class, and PATO has 'apiculate' only as a synonym of the sharpness attribute.

first_reason: Soft-wooded describes the wood, not the whole bearer. Mapping it to plain 'soft' loses the wood. The bearer should be wood.
reason: The softness belongs to the wood (PO secondary xylem, which has 'wood' as a synonym), not to the bearer named in the text. A word rule cannot move the quality to a different part, so this needs a pattern.

first_reason: Unpleasant alone can describe smell or taste. It is foetid only when the description is about smell.
reason: On its own, 'unpleasant' can describe taste as well as smell. FLOPO:0991020 foetid already has 'unpleasant smell' as a synonym, which covers the clear case.

first_reason: The quality 'inconspicuous' belongs to the veins, not to the bearer. The bearer should be vein, or the rule should be limited to veined parts.
reason: The quality 'inconspicuous' belongs to the veins (PO vascular bundle / vein), not to the leaf. This needs the pattern that puts the quality on the part's veins, not a word rule.

first_reason: Layered means stratified for tissues and coverings. For shoots or branches it can mean tiers, or layering as propagation.
reason: PATO stratified is right for layered tissues and coverings. For shoots or branches, 'layered' can mean tiered, or rooting by layering.

first_reason: Leafy loses 'densely'. Dense leaf arrangement is part of the meaning.
reason: A densely leaved shoot is leafy (FLOPO:0991012), so the mapping is true. It is less specific, but it does not say anything false, unlike 'sparsely leafy'.

first_reason: Cleft means cut about halfway, which is palmatifid, a subclass of palmately lobed. Palmately lobed loses the depth.
reason: 'Cleft' means cut about halfway, which matches the definition of FLOPO:0991351 palmatifid, a subclass of palmately lobed.

first_reason: Nervose means conspicuously veined, not just having veins. Vascular bundle present loses the 'prominent'. Consider rejecting.
reason: 'Nervose' means conspicuously veined. 'Vascular bundle present' is true of almost every leaf, so it loses the whole meaning. FLOPO has no prominently-veined class.

first_reason: Long-ovate means elongate ovate, and ovate loses the elongation. Ovate-oblong is a different shape.
reason: A long-ovate outline is still egg-shaped and broadest below the middle, so it falls under FLOPO:0991024 ovate. Only the narrowness is lost, and nothing false is stated.

first_reason: Prominent loses the convex shape of the raised part.
reason: PATO prominent (standing out or projecting beyond a surface) is true of a convexly raised part. Only the convex outline is lost.

first_reason: Well spaced means evenly spaced, not widely separated. Distant means far apart. Reject the rule.
reason: In floras, 'well spaced' (flowers, leaves, veins) means clearly separated, not crowded. That matches FLOPO:0991189 distant. Evenly spaced is a different class (FLOPO:0991365) and is not what 'well' means.

first_reason: Insignificant means inconspicuous only for showy parts. For other parts it can simply mean small.
reason: For flowers and their parts, 'insignificant' means not showy, which is PATO inconspicuous. For other parts it can just mean small or unimportant.

first_reason: 'Expanding' usually describes growth or unfolding in time, as in 'expanding leaves'. It does not mean dilated. Reject the word.
reason: 'Expanding' is ambiguous: it can describe growth over time ('expanding leaves') or widening along a part ('expanding into a sheath'). It does not reliably mean PATO dilated.

first_reason: Bristles are only one kind of trichome. Bristleless does not mean there are no trichomes at all. The target needs 'bristle absent'.
reason: 'Bristle' is a synonym of both PO trichome and PO awn, and in Asteraceae it means pappus bristles. 'Bristleless' does not mean all trichomes are absent.

first_reason: 'Not produced' is a generic phrase, for example 'not produced beyond the apex'. It does not mean not excurrent. Reject the word.
reason: 'Not produced' is a general phrase ('not produced beyond the apex'). It has no fixed link to FLOPO:0991162 excurrent.

first_reason: Bigeniculate means bent twice (a twice-kneed awn). 'Bent' loses the 'twice'.
reason: A twice-kneed awn is bent (PATO bent), so the mapping is true. FLOPO has no geniculate class to use instead. Only 'twice' is lost.

first_reason: 'Long' is lost. A long awn is more specific than an awn being present. Map to awn present plus a length value, or reject.
reason: Long-aristate entails having an arista, which PO awn has as a synonym, so 'awn present' is true. The length is lost but nothing false is stated.

first_reason: Striate-veined says the veins form fine parallel lines. 'Striated' alone loses the link to venation. Better 'veins striate' on the vein bearer, or reject.
reason: The striation belongs to the venation, not the bearer. Putting PATO striated on the bearer is wrong without the vein pattern.

first_reason: Semi-exserted means only partly projecting. Mapping it to exserted loses the 'partly'. Reject, or keep as a phrase for review.
reason: 'Semi-exserted' means only partly projecting. PATO exserted would say the part fully projects, which the text does not say.

first_reason: Laminated means in thin layers, which fits stratified only for layered structures. On leaves it can mean lamina-like.
reason: PATO stratified fits 'laminated' only for structures made of thin layers. On leaves, the word can refer to the lamina (blade).

first_reason: Lax-flowered means flowers loosely arranged on an inflorescence. The loose quality belongs to the inflorescence, and the bearer 'flower' is lost. Use inflorescence + loose, or reject.
reason: In 'inflorescence lax-flowered' the bearer is the inflorescence, which the statement already names, and PATO loose (PATO_0001802; related synonym lax) is exactly right. Accepted siblings use the same mapping: laxly, laxiflorous and laxly arranged all go to loose. The flowers are not the bearer.

first_reason: Acrid means pungent or burning, not bitter. Use a pungent class if one exists, otherwise reject.
reason: The PATO definition of bitter (PATO_0002474) is literally 'an acrid, sharp, or disagreeable flavor', so acrid taste of sap, tubers or leaves is covered. There is no pungent class in PATO or FLOPO. 'Acrid smell' would be odorous (PATO_0001331), but a part-name constraint cannot catch that, and it is rare.

first_reason: Glomerule is a noun for a dense cluster of flowers, which is a bearer or inflorescence type. It is not the quality capitate. The quality form would be glomerate.
reason: 'Flowers in glomerules' means flowers in dense clusters, often sessile and axillary (Amaranthaceae, Urticaceae). These are not heads on a shortened inflorescence axis, which is what FLOPO capitate requires. The accepted rule R0233 maps glomerate to PATO aggregated (exact synonym 'clustered'), the parent of capitate. The PO synonym glomerule on compound capitulum (PO_0030122) is the Asteraceae sense and does not fit general use.

first_reason: Decreasing is ambiguous because it can mean size or number. Tapered size fits only for organs that get smaller along an axis.
reason: Tapered size (PATO_0005015) is a size gradient along a set of parts: 'leaves decreasing upwards', 'pinnae decreasing towards the base'. On other bearers 'decreasing' can mean decreasing in number or in some other quality, so keep it to serial leaf-like parts.

first_reason: 'Divided almost' is a fragment of 'divided almost to the base'. The depth is lost, and the word on its own is not a quality. Reject, or handle as a phrase.
reason: Whatever follows the fragment ('to the base', 'to the middle', 'to the midrib'), the part is divided, so PATO split (PATO_0001786, 'divided into parts or divisions') is true in every reading. The depth is lost, as other kept rules lose a modifier. Parted (FLOPO_0991234) would be wrong for 'almost to the middle'.

first_reason: Marine means living in the sea, so salt water is lost. Aquatic is a parent term, but the rule needs a marine or saline class or manual review.
reason: Marine plants (seagrasses, marine herbs) grow submerged in sea water, which FLOPO aquatic (FLOPO_0991112) covers: growing wholly or partly in water. Salinity is a habitat detail outside PATO's scope, and no saline class exists. Aquatic is a correct broader term, not a wrong one.

first_reason: Cincinnate describes an inflorescence or branching that is a cincinnus (scorpioid). It is not a presence of a separate part, so keep it to inflorescence-type bearers.
reason: This uses the same pattern as the accepted rule R0023 (dichasial maps to cyme inflorescence present). PO lists cincinni, scorpioid and monochasium as synonyms of cincinnus inflorescence (PO_0030132), so 'cymes cincinnate' names that inflorescence type. The word only occurs with inflorescences, so a part constraint adds nothing.

first_reason: Ill-defined means indistinct or not sharply delimited, as with margins or limits. It does not mean inconspicuous (hard to see).
reason: For veins, 'ill-defined' means faint or not clearly visible, which is inconspicuous (PATO_0000464), as the accepted rule maps 'obscurely veined' to inconspicuous. For margins, zones and inflorescences it means 'not sharply delimited', which inconspicuous does not cover and no class does.

first_reason: Pilose means long soft hairs. Glandular-pubescent says short soft hairs plus glands, so the hair type is lost.
reason: Glandular-pubescent (FLOPO_0991173) requires short soft hairs, but pilose means long hairs, so the rule is wrong. No glandular-pilose class exists. Pilose (FLOPO_0991048) alone would lose the glands, and glandular (PATO_0002117) alone would lose the hair type. It needs a new class or two separate annotations, not this rule.

first_reason: Fully developed is the opposite of undeveloped or immature. It is not the opposite of vestigial. Do not map it.
reason: 'Fully developed' is mostly a stage word ('fully developed leaves/fruits'), which belongs to the stage pattern, not to a quality. Only occasionally does it contrast with a reduced staminode. 'Not vestigial' is not what the text says.

first_reason: The word 'long' (length of the sheath) is lost when this is mapped to plain sheathing.
reason: The core quality is sheathing (FLOPO_0991105). 'Long' only grades the length of the sheath, like 'high' in high-conic (R1762) and 'erect' in erect-appressed (R0673), both kept. The sheath length can be recorded as its own measure.

first_reason: Buried means subterranean only for organs that sit in soil. 'Seeds buried in pulp' would be wrong.
reason: Subterranean (FLOPO_0991035) is right for organs buried in soil, and for fruits in geocarpic species such as Arachis. 'Seeds buried in pulp', 'stomata buried' and 'glands buried in tissue' are not subterranean, so limit the rule to soil organs.

first_reason: Pea-like means a pea-type (papilionaceous) flower or a pea-like fruit. It does not mean that a keel is present.
reason: PO defines keel (PO_0025327) as the two lowest petals of a papilionaceous corolla. A pea-like flower or corolla is papilionaceous, so 'keel present' carries that type. 'Fruit pea-like' (pea-sized) and 'seed pea-like' do not, so limit the rule to flowers and corollas.

first_reason: Broomlike means many slender erect twigs. That is close to virgate, but only for the plant, stems and branches.
reason: FLOPO virgate (FLOPO_0991038) has 'broom-like' as a synonym and fits plants, stems and branches with many slender erect twigs. This matches the sibling rule R0819 (broom-like, limited to whole plant|plant|shrub|habit). The corona-appendage use is not virgate.

first_reason: Not splitting usually describes a fruit that does not open, which is not dehiscent. PATO 'split' means clefted, which is a different meaning.
reason: Keep the rule as a negation, but negate dehiscent ('opening at maturity to release its contents'): a fruit 'not splitting' does not open. PATO split (PATO_0001786) is a cut or cleft shape, which is a different character, so 'not split' is wrong.

first_reason: 'Low' makes the shape flat or shallow, a different form from plain conical.
reason: A low-conic stylopodium or operculum is still cone-shaped. 'Low' only grades the height, as 'high' does in the accepted rule high-conic maps to conical (R1762). Conical (PATO_0002021) is right.

first_reason: Setulose means bearing small bristles, which are stiff. Pubescent means soft hairs, so these are different indumentum types.
reason: Setulose means bearing small stiff bristles, but glandular-pubescent (FLOPO_0991173) means soft hairs, so the rule is wrong. No glandular-setulose class exists. Setose (PATO_0002289) would lose the glands and glandular (PATO_0002117) would lose the bristles.

first_reason: The word gives a count of veins. 'Vascular bundle present' loses the number and says nothing a veined part would not already say.
reason: This matches the accepted rule R0868 (multiveined maps to vascular bundle present) and the 'veined' rule C211. 'Several' is not a number, so the count pattern cannot hold it. What the word reliably says is that veins are present.

first_reason: The word means erect and also pressed against the surface. Appressed alone loses 'erect'.
reason: Appressed (FLOPO_0991064) is the defining content. Pressed flat against an upward-running axis already implies the erect direction, as the rule's own reason says. 'Erect' adds nothing, and there is no compound class.

first_reason: Bulged only means swollen or protruding. Gibbous means swollen on one side, which is narrower.
reason: 'Bulged' means swollen or protruding, but not necessarily on one side. Gibbous (FLOPO_0991130) requires one-sided swelling, so it is too narrow. PATO swollen is already used for flora 'swollen' bases and nodes, as the accepted pairs in flora_union_pairs.tsv show.

first_reason: Converging means leaning toward each other. Connivent also says the parts touch without fusing, and the word 'converging' does not say that. Convergent would be the better target if one exists.
reason: Connivent (FLOPO_0991147) requires the parts to converge and touch. 'Converging' only says they lean toward each other, as stamens or follicles do. Neither PATO nor FLOPO has a convergent class, so no existing class fits.

first_reason: Gummy means exuding or covered with gum or resin. Viscid only means sticky and loses the gum.
reason: A gummy bud, leaf or fruit surface is sticky with exudate, which is PATO viscid (PATO_0001370), a sticky coating. Resinous (FLOPO_0991075) would be wrong because gum is not resin. The kind of exudate is a chemical detail.

first_reason: 'Sharply defined' describes a distinct margin or limit, not conspicuousness. It has no good existing target.
reason: For veins, 'sharply defined' means distinct or clearly visible, which matches the existing reading of 'veins distinct' and 'vein visible' as conspicuous (PATO_0000463, R2040). For colour zones, margins and borders it means 'clearly delimited', which conspicuous does not cover. This mirrors R0594.

first_reason: The rule loses the round shape. Round-raised is a raised, rounded structure, and prominent says nothing about shape.
reason: 'Raised' is what prominent (PATO_0001482) means: standing out beyond a surface. This matches the accepted 'bulging' rule (R0021). 'Round' grades the form of the raised area, as 'low' does in low-conic. The shape can be added separately but is not needed for the rule.

first_reason: Vestigial means a rudimentary remnant. Scarcely developed only means barely developed, which is weaker.
reason: An aril, calyx tube or pistil that is scarcely developed is reduced to a trace. Accepted rules read obsolete (C234), rudimentary (C142), obsolescent (R0690) and subnul (R0853/R1989) the same way, as vestigial (PATO_0000588).

first_reason: Biparous (a biparous cyme) means two lateral branches under the terminal flower, a dichasium. It is not bifurcated.
reason: A biparous cyme is a dichasium, and PO lists dichasium as a synonym of cyme inflorescence. The rule should become an entity-presence rule ('cyme inflorescence present'), the same as R0023 dichasial. Bifurcated (PATO_0001784) is wrong.

first_reason: 'Pale' is lost. Chestnut colour alone is not pale chestnut-brown.
reason: Chestnut-brown is an exact synonym of chestnut colour (PATO_0104329). 'Pale' is a lightness modifier, as in the accepted rule R1850 (light straw-colored maps to straw yellow). PATO has no pale chestnut class.

first_reason: Hypocrepiform means horseshoe-shaped. Salverform is hypocrateriform, a different word. No class for the right shape was found.
reason: Hypocrepiform means horseshoe-shaped. It is not hypocrateriform, which is salverform (FLOPO_0991144). No horseshoe-shape class exists in PATO or FLOPO. It needs a new class or should be rejected.

first_reason: The target is a leaf midvein. On a sepal, bract or petal the midrib is not a leaf midvein.
reason: PO gives midrib as an exact synonym of leaf midvein (PO_0020139), but that class is for leaves only. On sepals, bracts, glumes or valves the target should be vascular bundle (PO_0005020), and in mosses the costa (PO_0030072). The accepted rules for midvein (R1773) and midnerved (R1472) say the same.

first_reason: Nervous means with visible veins (nerves). This holds for flat parts, and PO lists vein as a synonym of vascular bundle. It is doubtful for other parts.
reason: Botanical 'nervous' (nervosus) means nerved. Accepted rules map its variants (nervate R0115, nervose R0478, nervured R1357) to vascular bundle present with no part constraint, and veins occur on stems and fruits as well as flat parts. 'Énerviées' (nerveless) belongs to the 'nerveless' rule.

first_reason: Supra-axillary means above the axil. Extra-axillary only means outside the axil, so the position is lost.
reason: Supra-axillary (arising above the axil) is a kind of extra-axillary (arising outside the axil), so the mapping is true, only less specific. With 7 statements a rule is enough. 'Above' is a finer position that has no term.

first_reason: The arcuate (curved) form of the ascent is lost. The curved form would need a second quality.
reason: Ascending (PATO:0104355) covers parts directed obliquely upward. 'Arcuately' only says how the curve runs and can be dropped, as other accepted rules do (e.g. 'longitudinally fissured' -> fissured). The mapping is true.

first_reason: Columellate is a pollen exine term (rod-like columellae). PO columella is a different structure, for example the moss capsule columella.
reason: In the floras 'columellate' describes pollen exine (rod-like columellae) and lichen apothecia. PO_0025230 columella covers fruit and moss-capsule columellae, which are different structures, and no PO class fits the other senses.

first_reason: Reticulate is lost. The word means a net pattern with pits, so it needs both reticulate and alveolate.
reason: The definition of FLOPO:0991203 alveolate (close-set angular pits like a honeycomb) already implies a network of walls between the pits. 'Reticulate' only names those walls, so nothing important is lost.

first_reason: Excised means cut out, not a notched apex. Emarginate is a specific shape of a tip and the two are not the same.
reason: Glossaries give 'excised' as 'with a notch cut out'. On an apex, tip or edge that is PATO:0002234 emarginate ('having a notched tip or edge'). On other parts the word can mean 'cut away' more generally.

first_reason: The bearer (nerves or veins) is lost. The meaning is that the venation is inconspicuous, so it needs the nerve or vein as bearer.
reason: A plain pato rule puts the quality on the part named in the sentence, so 'leaves obscurely nerved' would give 'leaf inconspicuous', which is false. The rule kind cannot set the veins (PO:0005020) as the part. 'Obscure' (C174) already covers 'obscure veins', where the veins are named.

first_reason: Narrow-necked only says the neck is narrow. Flask-shaped also says the body is swollen below, and that is not stated.
reason: Flask-shaped (FLOPO:0991183) needs a body swollen below plus a neck. 'Narrow-necked' states only the neck, and the rule's own note found a case that does not fit. Too doubtful for 4 statements.

first_reason: Petiolelike means resembling a petiole or stalk. Attenuate means tapering gradually to a point, which is a different thing.
reason: In 'leaf base narrowed and petiolelike', the taper comes from 'narrowed'. 'Petiolelike' alone means stalk-like (e.g. a pseudopetiole or claw), not 'tapering to a slender point' as PATO:0001982 attenuate is defined.

first_reason: The bare word tearing does not mean fragile. It can describe how a part splits or opens, or the action of tearing. Fragile needs an explicit statement such as breaking easily.
reason: Fragile fits only 'readily tearing'. The bare word also describes how spathes or sheaths split or open (dehiscence), so the rule is ambiguous.

first_reason: Knob-shaped can describe a swelling anywhere on a part. Head-shaped is defined as abruptly enlarged at the tip into a rounded head.
reason: A knob-shaped stigma or hair tip is head-shaped (FLOPO:0991097: abruptly enlarged at the tip into a rounded head; the term already applies to stigma and trichome). On other parts a knob can be a swelling anywhere.

first_reason: Nodule-bearing means root nodules for roots. Leaf and stem nodules also occur, for example bacterial leaf nodules in Psychotria, so the rule should not apply to other parts.
reason: Root nodule present (PO_0003023) is right only for roots and plants. Nodules on leaves (bacterial leaf nodules) are not root nodules. The rule's own note says it is for roots only.

first_reason: Broom-like means many slender erect twigs, as in a broom. Virgate means wand-like, which is long, slender, straight and erect.
reason: The rule already applies only to whole plants. Virgate (FLOPO:0991038) lists 'broom-like' as a related synonym. A broom-like shrub (e.g. Retama, Cytisus) is one with many slender, straight, erect twigs, which is the virgate habit.

first_reason: The rule loses the position (centrally). The statement says only that the part is not constricted in the middle.
reason: It negates constricted. For an aroid spathe, constriction would be in the middle (between tube and blade), so 'not constricted' says the same thing. The rule's note says the region (centrally) is handled separately.

first_reason: Pilulose is not a clear synonym of puberulous. It is rare and can mean bearing small ball-like bodies, so the mapping is doubtful.
reason: Glossaries give 'pilulose' as minutely pilose (very small, fine hairs), which falls under puberulous (FLOPO:0991049: very short, fine, soft hairs). It is not 'pilular' (ball-shaped). With 66 statements, the hair sense is the one the floras use.

first_reason: Without keels says the keel structure is missing. It does not say the shape is not keel-shaped. This should be an entity-absence rule, not a negated shape.
reason: This matches the accepted rules R0450, R0606 and R0640, which map 'not keeled', 'ecarinate' and 'without keel' to 'not keel-shaped'. In glumes, lemmas and fruits the keel is a ridge, not a separate part. PO_0025327 keel is the pea-family petal keel, so an absence rule would use the wrong class.

first_reason: Keelless means no keel. It does not mean not keel-shaped, so it should be an absence rule.
reason: Same as R0830 and R0606 (ecarinate): keelless means not carinate. PO keel is the pea-family petal keel and cannot be used here.

first_reason: Rampant means vigorous and spreading unchecked. It does not mean creeping along the ground.
reason: In the French floras, 'rampant(e)' on axes and plants means creeping (FLOPO:0991009, synonym repent). The English sense 'growing vigorously' and use on other parts should not get the rule. These parts match the creeping term's own part list.

first_reason: Delimited means bounded or marked off by a limit. It does not mean conspicuous.
reason: Delimited means marked off or bounded, often by different cells (e.g. moss alar cells). It is not visibility of the part. The bare key would also fire inside 'poorly delimited'.

first_reason: Nigrescent means turning black or blackish. Black loses the becoming or tending part.
reason: Nigrescent means blackish or turning black. A tint near black is still black (PATO:0000317), and the 'when dry' and stage readings are handled by the existing pattern for specimen condition (docs/odp/06-specimen-condition.md) and by stage words.

first_reason: Sheathed can mean enclosed by a sheath. Sheathing means wrapping round an axis. Not sheathed does not clearly negate the wrapping quality.
reason: 'Sheathed' usually means enclosed by a sheath (passive), while FLOPO:0991105 sheathing means the part itself wraps the axis. 'Not sheathed' (e.g. spines 'neither sheathed nor barbed') does not clearly negate sheathing.

first_reason: Shreddy normally describes bark that peels in shreds. The exfoliating term is for bark and axes, not other parts.
reason: Shreddy bark peeling in strips fits exfoliating (FLOPO:0991021), which is defined for bark and the axes that carry it. On other parts (e.g. fibrous leaf sheaths) 'shreddy' is fibrous tearing, not exfoliation.

first_reason: Multicipital means many-headed, with a stem base or caudex that branches into many heads. It is not branching in general.
reason: Multicipital (many-headed) is branching of a caudex, rootstock or taproot crown into several heads. Branched (PATO:0000402) is true for those parts only.

first_reason: Thinned can mean made thin, but it can also mean reduced in density or number. It only means decreased thickness for plain parts.
reason: On margins, walls and blades 'thinned' (French 'aminci') means thinner, i.e. decreased thickness. On other parts (e.g. a thinned indumentum) it can mean less dense.

first_reason: The word includes its bearer, the stem. A rule on decreased strength alone loses that the stem is the weak part. It should be stem + decreased strength.
reason: The word is said of the plant, and a pato rule cannot move the quality to the stem. The result would be 'whole plant decreased strength', which is wrong. It needs a rule kind or pattern that sets stem (PO_0009047) as the part.

first_reason: Daisy-like means radiate only for composite heads or flowers.
reason: Radiate (FLOPO:0991194) is defined for a capitulum with ray flowers. Also, 'daisy-like flowers' appears in non-composites (e.g. Aizoaceae), where radiate is false, so 'flower' is left out.

first_reason: Pennate means pinnately veined only on a blade or leaflet. On a whole leaf it often means pinnate, with leaflets.
reason: 'Nervation pennée' and pennate blades or leaflets are pinnately veined (FLOPO:0991201). For a whole leaf, 'pennate' can mean pinnate with leaflets, so leaf is left out.

first_reason: Multiveined means many veins, which is a count. 'Vascular bundle present' loses the 'many'. It should not be mapped without the count.
reason: Multiveined implies veined, and this matches the accepted rules C211 and C212 ('veined', 'nerved' -> vascular bundle present). The statement is true. 'Many' is not a number the counting rules can take, so leaving it out loses detail without making it false.

first_reason: Long-rhomboidal means elongate rhombic. Rhomboid alone loses the elongation.
reason: An elongate rhomb is still rhomboid (PATO:0001938). 'Long' is a degree within the shape, handled as in 'depressed-globose'. The mapping is true for the moss leaf cells it describes.

first_reason: Deep-seated means subterranean only for underground organs. Other parts, such as glands or veins, can also be deep-seated.
reason: For underground organs, deep-seated means well below the soil surface, which is subterranean (FLOPO:0991035). Glands, veins or cells can also be deep-seated (sunken), and that is not this position.

first_reason: Graceful is an aesthetic word and does not mean slender. No safe target exists.
reason: 'Graceful' describes how a part looks. PATO slender lists 'gracile' only as a related synonym, and for whole plants the word is vague. Too doubtful for a rule.

first_reason: Auricles also occur on leaf blades, not only on the sheath, so this is only right for grass-like leaves. The part must be a leaf or sheath.
reason: PO leaf sheath auricle fits the grass blades and culm sheaths that are most of the examples. Petal and leaf-base auricles have no PO class. For those, 'exauriculate' already maps to not auriculate (R0625), so this rule should not reach them.

first_reason: Pale-speckled adds a pale colour of the spots. Spotted alone loses it.
reason: Speckled = spotted (C334). 'Pale' is the colour of the spots, a detail of the spots that can be stated about them. This follows linear-foveolate and the tinged colours, where the main quality is kept and the modifier is dropped.

first_reason: Mutic means without an awn or point, and it is used for grass parts. On other parts it can mean having no mucro or spine.
reason: Same as muticous/awnless/unawned (C348, R1196) on grass parts. On leaf apices, achenes or sepals, mutique means without a mucro or point, not without an awn.

first_reason: Sarmentous means with long, slender, trailing or runner-like stems. That is not always climbing.
reason: Sarmentous is the French 'sarmenteux', meaning long flexible stems that lean on or scramble through other plants. It is reviewed as climbing for sarmentose (R0155, with this same part constraint) and for sarmenteux (R1460). Use the same parts for consistency.

first_reason: Linear-foveolate means small pits in a linear arrangement. Foveate loses the linear arrangement.
reason: Foveate (pitted) is the quality. The long shape of the pits is a detail of the pits and does not need its own class. Modifiers like this are dropped the same way elsewhere, for example 'longitudinally fissured' becomes fissured.

first_reason: A falsely petiolate leaf has a narrowed base that looks like a petiole (a pseudopetiole). It does not mean the whole leaf tapers. Leave it unmapped or reject it.
reason: FLOPO_0991298 petiole-like is defined as a leaf blade base narrowed into a stalk resembling a petiole, and it has 'pseudopetiolate' as a synonym. That is exactly 'falsely petiolate'. Tapered loses the stalk-like base.

first_reason: Geocarpic means the fruit ripens underground, so it only applies to fruiting parts. Subterranean is the closest class for them.
reason: Geocarpic fruits ripen below the ground surface, which is FLOPO subterranean on the fruit. On the whole plant or a peduncle it describes a behaviour, not being underground. Seeds are covered through the fruit.

first_reason: Eporose means without pores. Pores are not the same as perforations (perforate), so not perforate loses the meaning. Pore absence on the bearer is more exact.
reason: The examples are walls of moss leaf cells with no pores, meaning holes through the wall. PO has no class for a cell-wall pore, so 'pore absent' cannot be stated. 'Not perforate' (no holes) is the closest negation that exists.

first_reason: Limbless fits leaf lamina absent only for leaf-like parts. For petals or a corolla, limb means something else.
reason: 'Sans limbe' on leaves, sheaths and cataphylls means without a blade, as in the reviewed 'bladeless' rule. For a calyx or corolla, the limb is the spreading upper part (calyx limb FLOPO_0986093, perianth limb FLOPO_0986104), not a leaf lamina.

first_reason: Villoso-ciliate means villous and ciliate. Mapping to ciliated alone loses the villous hairs. Split it into two qualities, or leave it unmapped.
reason: This means a margin fringed with long soft hairs, so ciliated is the quality and is correct. 'Villoso-' only names the kind of hair. Villous (FLOPO_0991051) can be added as a second value, but the mapping as it stands is not wrong.

first_reason: Interconnected means anastomosing only for veins and similar networks. For other parts it just means connected.
reason: Anastomosing (branches rejoining into a network) fits interconnected veins and fern rhizomes. Elsewhere, for example connate parts or connected cells, it only means joined.

first_reason: Scattered describes how things are arranged. Sparse describes how few there are. The two are not the same.
reason: PATO sparse (PATO_0001609) is defined as 'scattered; spread irregularly, and at a distance from each other', which is exactly this phrase. This is the same as the reviewed 'sparsely scattered' (R1595) and 'sparsely distributed' (R1873).

first_reason: Functionally staminate means the flower has some female parts but acts as male. Plain 'male' loses the word 'functionally'.
reason: This follows 'staminate' (C233) and the reviewed bearer rules R3370-R3372: PO staminate flower allows a gynoecium that aborted during development. 'Functionally' only notes that the female parts are rudimentary.

first_reason: Scattered-pilose means sparsely hairy. Plain pilose loses the sparse density.
reason: Pilose is the quality. 'Scattered' or 'sparsely' is a word of degree kept in the record. This is the same as 'sparsely pubescent' (R0080) and 'sparsely hirsute' (R1502). FLOPO pilose is itself defined with scattered hairs.

first_reason: Dehiscence is the process or the mode of opening. It does not say the part is dehiscent. It can come with 'indehiscent' or 'by slits'.
reason: In the quality field, 'dehiscence (along a suture / transversale)' says the part opens, which is dehiscent. This matches 'dehiscing' (R0096). Indehiscent and more specific ways of opening have their own rules.

first_reason: The target is the secondary vein of a leaf. Other parts such as petals or bracts also have lateral veins.
reason: PO secondary leaf vein is a vein of a leaf. On lemmas, glumes, petals or bracts, lateral veins are not leaf veins and need a different anatomy class.

first_reason: Increasing is generic, for example in size or number. Accrescent means a part that keeps growing after flowering, such as the calyx.
reason: 'Increasing' on its own is a general word: increasing in size, number or diameter, or a change along the part. Accrescent applies only when the text names it or says the part enlarges after flowering, and those cases have their own rules.

first_reason: Densely clothed means densely covered with hairs or indumentum. Plain dense loses what covers the surface.
reason: Density is the quality of the covering. What does the covering (hairs, scales) is a separate statement, as the previous review held for 'covered'.

first_reason: Tooth-shaped means dentiform. It is not necessarily triangular.
reason: Tooth-shaped (dentiform) is about how a part looks, not a fixed outline. Teeth can be narrow, hooked or rounded, so triangular claims too much. There is no dentiform class in PATO or FLOPO, and with only 7 statements a new term is not worth adding.

first_reason: Irregularly quadrate is not a regular square. The 'irregularly' is lost.
reason: Quadrate moss leaf cells are square. 'Irregularly' only loosens the value, as an approximate value under pattern 01, the same way 'tinged' and '-ish' are handled.

first_reason: Pseudo-axillary means only apparently axillary, not truly axillary. Extra-axillary means outside the axil, and the 'apparently' is lost. Keep the rule only if no better term exists.
reason: A pseudo-axillary inflorescence (for example in Solanaceae) truly arises outside the axil and only looks axillary. That is what FLOPO extra-axillary states. No closer term exists.

first_reason: Glandular-tipped describes hairs with a gland at the tip. That is stipitate-glandular, not a glandular-pubescent indumentum.
reason: In 'hairs glandular-tipped' the bearer is the hair, which has a gland at its tip. Handle it like the reviewed 'gland-tipped' rule (R0010): gland present at the apex. Glandular-pubescent describes a surface clothed with such hairs and is wrong on the hair itself. Stipitate-glandular has the same problem.

first_reason: 'Midvein extending' is ambiguous. It may extend beyond the apex (excurrent) or only to it. Percurrent means to the apex and not beyond, so this rule over-commits.
reason: The key leaves out where the vein ends. 'Midvein extending' can continue 'to the apex' (percurrent), 'beyond the apex' (excurrent, FLOPO_0991162) or 'to the middle'. Map the full phrases instead.

first_reason: Obcuneiform means inversely wedge-shaped, with the narrow end at the apex. Cuneate loses the 'ob-' and so reverses the orientation. Better as a new term, or reject.
reason: Glossaries define obcuneate/obcuneiform as wedge-shaped with the narrow end at the apex, the reverse of cuneate. Floras use it loosely, so the word is ambiguous. With 5 statements, reject rather than force cuneate.

first_reason: Geniculate means sharply bent like a knee. 'Not geniculate' may still be curved or bent, so 'not bent' is too strong.
reason: The previous review mapped geniculate to PATO bent (C191), and neither PATO nor FLOPO has a geniculate class. Its negation is therefore 'not bent', the same form as other negated values.

first_reason: Tinged purple means faintly or partly purple. Purple loses the 'slightly' meaning.
reason: This is the same as the reviewed 'purple tinged' (R0666), 'tinged brown' (R0991) and 'tinged reddish' (R1639): the colour is purple, and 'tinged' is a qualifier meaning 'approximately' under pattern 01.

first_reason: Defined means distinct or clearly delimited, such as a defined margin. It does not mean conspicuous.
reason: 'Clearly defined' veinlets and alar regions are clearly visible, the same reading as 'distinct' (C176) and 'well-defined' (R0160). 'Ill-defined' already maps to inconspicuous (R0594).

first_reason: 'Not clearly differentiated' means not distinct from a neighbouring part, for example calyx and corolla. It is not about conspicuousness.
reason: Moss alar cells or a central strand that are not clearly differentiated do not stand out from the cells around them. This is the same reading as 'ill-defined' and 'indistinct', which map to inconspicuous (R0594). PATO 'undifferentiated' is about cell maturity and does not fit.

first_reason: Sheath-less means the sheath is missing, so the entity is absent. 'Not sheathing' means the part does not clasp, which is a different claim. Use sheath absent.
reason: The examples are bracts whose base does not wrap round the axis. PO has a sheath class only for leaves, and the bare word 'sheath' was rejected as a generic part. So negating FLOPO sheathing is the best grounded reading for bracts. Leaf cases are covered by 'sheathless' (R0461).

first_reason: Defoliate means the leaves have been shed, which is a state or time-bound loss. It does not mean leaves are absent. Better as deciduous or leafless-at-time, or reject.
reason: 'Stems defoliate proximally' says the leaves are absent from the lower stem now. Where to put it on the stem comes from the part-of-bearer pattern, and words of time ('at flowering') come from context words. This is the same as 'aphyllous' (R0373).

first_reason: Compound corymb is a specific kind of inflorescence. Plain 'corymb present' loses 'compound'. Constrain it or leave unmapped.
reason: PO lists 'compound corymb' as a synonym of corymb inflorescence (PO_0030124), so mapping it to corymb present follows PO itself. The 'compound' detail is something PO also leaves out.

first_reason: A tendril-tipped rachis only exists on compound leaves. On a simple leaf the tendril is at the apex of the lamina.
reason: A tendril at the tip of the rachis (PO_0025366) exists only on compound leaves, as in Vicia and Lathyrus. On a simple leaf such as Gloriosa or Flagellaria, the tendril is a leaf apex tendril (PO_0025363), so a bare 'leaf' bearer is ambiguous.

first_reason: Variable-sized means size differs among individuals or samples. Unequal means parts differ within one structure. These are different characters.
reason: FLOPO unequal is defined for like parts within one set that differ in size. 'Variable-sized' in a taxon description often means variation between plants or specimens, which is a different character. The word is ambiguous between the two readings.

first_reason: A flared base means buttressed only for trees and trunks. On other parts it is not a buttress.
reason: On a trunk, having no flared base means having no buttresses, so 'not buttressed' (negation of FLOPO_0991138, as in the unbuttressed rule R0269) is safe. On corolla tubes, petioles and similar parts, 'flared base' has nothing to do with buttresses.

first_reason: Glandular papillate means papillae that are glandular. Mapping to papillose alone loses 'glandular'.
reason: The surface is still papillose (FLOPO_0991059), so the mapping is true even though 'glandular' is not carried. This follows R0355, where 'glandular puberulent' kept the main hair-cover term. The glandular detail can be added as a second annotation (PATO_0002117).

first_reason: Pleasant is a judgement of scent, not sweetness. A pleasant scent need not be sweet. The flower constraint also does not restrict it to scent.
