first_reason: A sinker is a specialised root, such as a descending parasitic or haustorial root, or a water-seeking root. PO root is too general. A bare 'sinker' can also mean a fishing weight or a fruit-tree shoot, so the word is ambiguous. Reject, or use a sinker-root class if one is created.
reason: A bare 'sinker' is ambiguous: in mistletoes (Loranthaceae, Viscaceae) it is the feeding organ that grows into the host (a haustorium), not a root, and elsewhere it is a descending root. No single class fits.

first_reason: A sinker root is a specific root type, usually a vertical root descending from a horizontal root. Mapping it to plain root loses that meaning. A constraint on the container would not fix it.
reason: A sinker root is a vertical root that grows down from a lateral root. PO has no narrower class, and mapping a narrower name to its PO parent is the normal pattern for bearer rules ('Narrower: ...'). PO root is correct, just less specific.

first_reason: Same as R3261: plural of sinker root, which is a specific kind of root.

first_reason: Bole is already a PO stem synonym and means the trunk of a tree. It is correct for trees and shrubs. It is wrong in the sense of a bole of a leaf bundle or a fungus-related use, and should not match other parts.

first_reason: A resin dot is a resin-filled gland or secretory cavity visible on the surface, and mapping it to 'portion of secretory tissue' loses the resin and the dot shape. PO lists 'gland' as a synonym of this class, so a resin-dot mapping is a stretch. Prefer a gland class, or reject.

first_reason: Same as R3267: a resin dot is a resin gland, not secretory tissue in general.
reason: Same as R3267.

first_reason: Same as R3267: the spaced form of resin-dot.
reason: Same as R3267, written with a space.

first_reason: A panicled cyme is a cyme arranged in a panicle, so it has both a cyme and a panicle part. PO cyme inflorescence loses the panicle arrangement, which is a quality of the inflorescence. first_reason: Same as R3270: 'paniculate cyme' loses the panicle arrangement.
reason: Same as R3270.

reason: PO has no sporangiophore class. PO sporophyll is 'a leaf-like organ bearing sporangia', but the stalked, shield-shaped (peltate) sporangiophores of Equisetum are not clearly leaf-like, and in fungi the word means something else. Leave unmapped or ask for a new class.

first_reason: Same as R3272: plural of sporangiophore, which is not a sporophyll.
reason: Plural of sporangiophore. Same as R3272.

first_reason: Costal veins are veins along the leaf margin or the main rib, as in grasses and palms. They are not the same as secondary veins. In some floras 'costal' secondary veins arise from the midrib, but this is not reliable.

first_reason: Same as R3279: plural of costal vein, which is not the same as secondary vein.
reason: Plural of costal vein. Same as R3279.

first_reason: Same as R3283: 'fruit head' is an infructescence of head form.
reason: Same as R3283: a fruit head is an infructescence, and the bearer is correct.

first_reason: Same as R3283: plural of fruiting head.

reason: Corolla lip (FLOPO_0985017) is right for the lower lip of a two-lipped corolla. Lamiaceae and Scrophulariaceae floras also give calyx lips, and an orchid lip is the labellum. Restrict the rule to corolla wholes, as done for 'lower lip lobe'.

first_reason: A lower lip is the anterior lip of a corolla, but 'lower lip' is also used for the calyx in Lamiaceae and for the orchid labellum. It is correct only when the whole is the corolla.

first_reason: Same as R3289: plural of floral scale.

first_reason: A calycophyll is a petaloid, enlarged calyx lobe, as in Mussaenda. It is a particular type of calyx lobe, so mapping it to a plain calyx lobe loses the enlarged, leaf-like form. Possibly acceptable only with a quality added.
reason: A calycophyll is a calyx lobe enlarged into a leaf-like blade. Mapping a kind of part to its parent class is acceptable for a bearer. Its shape, size, colour and hairs are correctly qualities of a calyx lobe.

first_reason: 'enlarged calyx lobe' includes a size quality (enlarged). Mapping it to calyx lobe alone drops the enlarged meaning. It should be calyx lobe plus a size quality.

first_reason: Same as R3298: plural of vascular strand.
reason: Plural of vascular strand. Same as R3298.

first_reason: A chalk gland is a gland that secretes calcium carbonate (lime scales), as in Saxifraga. It is a type of hydathode in some cases, but not all hydathodes secrete chalk. Mapping it to hydathode loses the chalk-secretion meaning, though the match is plausible.
reason: Lime-secreting pits on Saxifraga leaves are hydathodes, but the chalk glands of Plumbaginaceae are salt glands, not hydathodes. The gland class (PO synonym 'gland') is correct for both.

first_reason: 'Laminar' says the colleter sits on the leaf blade. The target loses that. Use colleter with leaf lamina as the container.

first_reason: Plural of 'laminar colleter'. The position on the leaf blade is lost.

first_reason: In Asteraceae the calyculus is a set of outer, short phyllaries, which are involucral bracts. In Malvaceae and Dipsacaceae the calyculus or epicalyx bracts are bracteoles below the calyx, which are plain bracts.

first_reason: Same as 'calicle bract'. Only correct for Asteraceae-type heads. Elsewhere it is an epicalyx bract (PO_0009055).
reason: Same as R3318. Outside Asteraceae heads it is an epicalyx segment.

first_reason: A pseudolocule is a false locule, a cavity without the true locule structure. Mapping it to locule loses the 'false' part.

first_reason: A false locule is not a true locule, and the 'false' part is lost.
reason: Same as R3327: a false locule is not a locule, and mapping it would give wrong locule counts.

first_reason: 'Pseudoloculed' is an adjective, meaning having false locules. It is a quality word, not a part name, so it should not be a bearer.

first_reason: A perianth blade is the limb of a fused perianth, not a tepal. No existing class fits it. Leave it unmapped, or use perianth with a limb container.

first_reason: This is the blade of a perianth segment, not the whole tepal. The 'blade' part is lost. A tepal lamina class would be better.
reason: Same as R3332. The blade part is lost, but the shape of the segment blade is the tepal shape as floras describe it, and no blade class exists.

first_reason: A coronal appendage is a structure on the corona (horn, scale, tooth), not the corona lobe itself.
reason: The statements describe separate members of a floral corona (ovate, bifid, spatulate, 6 mm long). The corona lobe definition, 'one of the divisions of a floral corona', with synonym 'coronal scale', fits them.

first_reason: A coronal appendage is a structure on the corona, not the corona lobe itself.
reason: Same as R3337. In floras, 'coronal appendage' names the separate members of the corona, as 'coronal scale' does.

first_reason: 'Tack-shaped' is a shape quality of the gland, and the rule would drop it. The bearer is the gland, and the shape stays as the quality.
reason: A tack-shaped gland is a gland (PO synonym). The shape word is not kept, but the bearer is correct, as already accepted for the 'tack-gland' rules R3339 and R3340.

first_reason: A spray is a branched inflorescence, but it can also be a leafy shoot or twig, so inflorescence is not always right.

first_reason: Plural of 'spray'. Same problem: it is not always an inflorescence.
reason: Plural of spray; same reasoning as R3342 (conifer foliage sprays must not become inflorescences).

first_reason: The word 'disk' carries the shape of the stigma, for example the Papaver stigmatic disc. Mapping to stigma loses it. Not mapped to stigma alone.
reason: In Nymphaeaceae the disk is not the stigma. In Nuphar the stigmatic disk is the flattened top of the ovary, with the stigmatic rays lying on it. In Nymphaea the stigmas sit in a cup, and the carpel tips (stigmatic appendages) stand around it. Its qualities in the data ('entire to crenate', 'occasionally reddened') are qualities of the disk margin and colour, not of the stigma. Papaver is the same: the disk is the sessile stigmatic cap of the ovary. Stigma (PO_0009073) is therefore wrong as the bearer. I could not check whether PO has a class for the ovary apex or a stigmatic region, so this word needs a new class or a 'stigma part of gynoecium' pattern, not a rule.

first_reason: 'Tubular flowers' mostly describes the corolla shape of any family, not Asteraceae disc flowers. Reject, or limit to Asteraceae heads.
reason: In Asteraceae heads the tubular florets are the disc florets (PO_0025332, synonym disc floret). Elsewhere 'tubular flowers' is a corolla-shape description of ordinary flowers. Map it only inside a head or capitulum.

first_reason: 'Fleurs tubuleuses' is a shape description used in many families. It is not only disc flowers.
reason: French form of R3375. 'Fleurs tubuleuses' are disc florets only inside an Asteraceae capitule; otherwise it describes a tubular corolla.

first_reason: 'Asexual reproductive body' is generic. It covers gemmae, bulbils, brood bodies and propagules. Gemma is only one kind.
reason: PO gemma (PO_0025614) is defined as a small ball of cells borne on a thallus. The data (Isopterygium, Pseudotaxiphyllum) describe uniseriate filamentous axillary propagula on leafy mosses, which do not fit that definition. The phrase also covers bulbils and brood bodies. No single existing class fits.

first_reason: Ostiole is the fig opening only in Ficus. Other plants and fungi have ostioles too, for example perithecia and algal conceptacles.
reason: In Ficus the ostiole is the syconium opening (the data include 'fruit: ostiole 4-5 mm diam.' and 'ostiole bilabié'). But Carex treatments use 'ostiole margin' for the mouth of the perigynium beak (eflora-fop), and fungal or algal ostioles exist too. Map it only when a fig or receptacle part is the context.

first_reason: 'Secondary rachis' also names an inflorescence axis in palms and grasses. It is the pinna rachis only on a compound leaf or frond.
reason: In ferns (Lygodium, Dryoathyrium) the secondary rachis is the pinna rachis. The data also have Ilex 'secondary rachis glabrate', which is an inflorescence axis, and palm and grass panicles use the term the same way.

first_reason: Same as R3395.
reason: Spelling variant of R3395; same constraint.

first_reason: French form of secondary rachis. Same as R3395.
reason: French form of R3395; it means the pinna rachis only on a compound leaf or frond, not on an inflorescence.

first_reason: A bare 'plica' also names folds of leaves, calyces and palm blades. It means a corolla plica only on the corolla.
reason: As a noun naming a bearer with its own shape, margin and size ('plicae broadly triangular', 'margin denticulate', 'plica apex acute'), 'plica' in the floras is the Gentianaceae corolla plica (Gentiana, Crawfurdia). first_reason: A bare 'plicae' is as generic as 'plica'. It is a corolla plica only on the corolla.
reason: Plural of plica; the data are Gentiana and Crawfurdia corolla plicae ('plicae broadly triangular, 2-4 mm long'). See R3406.

first_reason: I found no botanical meaning of 'stegidia' that equals stelidium. It is probably a misspelling or a different structure, so it is better rejected.
reason: All occurrences are Bulbophyllum (FDAC 'stégidies', plazi B. anjozorobeense) with stelidium qualities: lateral column teeth that are tapering, triangular, filiform, 0.5-3 mm long, flattened and curved forward. It is the form of 'stelidia' used in that flora, not a different structure.

first_reason: 'Anther appendix' can be a connective appendage, but it can also be a thecal or apical appendage. It is safer to keep it only where the connective is meant.
reason: In floras, 'anther appendix' is the apical membranous appendage of the connective, as in Apocynaceae/Asclepiadoideae (data: Ruehssia 'apical membranous appendix') and Melastomataceae. Thecal outgrowths are usually called awns, spurs or tails. A constraint of 'connective|anther' would add nothing, because the word already contains 'anther'.

first_reason: Anther tails are often thecal, as in Ericaceae, not connective. The word does not always mean a connective appendage.
reason: Anther tails are usually basal extensions of the thecae (Asteraceae caudate anthers, Ericaceae), not connective appendages. There is no existing thecal-appendage class, so no rule should map this word.

first_reason: A stigma head is a capitate stigma, not the head of the style. The right target is the stigma (or a stigma shape quality), not this class.
reason: In Apocynaceae treatments (Flora of China Asclepiadaceae, FTEA, Flora Zambesiaca), 'stigma head' (stigma-head) is the standard name for the style head (clavuncle), and that is where the phrase occurs as a bearer. A capitate stigma elsewhere is described as 'stigma capitate', not 'stigma head'.

first_reason: Pistil head is vague. It could mean the stigma, the style apex or the ovary top, so it should not map to style head.
reason: All data are Apocynaceae (Adenium obesum, Alafia caudata, Mascarenhasia arborescens: 'pistil head almost conical, 1-1.5 mm long'), where pistil head is the style head.

first_reason: Interstaminal appendages are any appendages between the stamens. They include corona parts, filament appendages and staminodes, so they are not always pseudostaminodes.
reason: Pseudostaminode is mainly an Amaranthaceae term. 'Interstaminal appendage' is broader: it also covers interstaminal staminodes (Sapotaceae), filament-tube teeth and corona lobes. There is also a conflict: R2353 already maps 'pseudo-staminode' to staminode (PO_0009077). Do not add a third route.

first_reason: Corolla scales include fornices, throat scales and corona scales, not only scales below the stamens.
reason: 'Corolla scale' covers Cuscuta infrastaminal scales, Boraginaceae fornices (already faucal appendage, FLOPO_0986115), Caryophyllaceae and Sapindaceae petal scales, and coronal scales. No single class fits.

first_reason: Fruit article also describes schizocarp parts, such as Brassicaceae lomentaceous fruits and Apiaceae mericarps, which are not loment segments. It would fit only for legume pods.
reason: 'Article' of a fruit is the segment of a lomentaceous fruit (Aeschynomene, Desmodium, Ormocarpum; data: 'articles semicircular, 1 or 2 articles'). The segments of lomentaceous Brassicaceae fruits are loment segments too. Apiaceae mericarps are not called articles.

first_reason: Fruit segment often means a citrus or other locule segment, or a mericarp. It is not a loment segment.
reason: The data already mix meanings. Monanthotaxis (Annonaceae) has segments of moniliform monocarps ('segments globose'), and Ormocarpum has loment joints. 'Fruit segment' is also used for mericarps and citrus segments.

first_reason: Trap also names the traps of Nepenthes, Dionaea, Genlisea, Sarracenia and Aldrovanda, not only bladders. It fits only for Utricularia and related bladderworts.
reason: All flora data are Utricularia (35+ statements: 'traps globose, glandular, 1-2 mm long, mouth basal'). The other trap genera (Dionaea, Aldrovanda, Genlisea) are rare in these floras, and Nepenthes and Sarracenia are described as pitchers, not traps.

first_reason: Plural of trap, with the same problem: it covers non-bladder traps.
reason: Plural of trap; same evidence as R3482 (Utricularia 'Traps numerous, globose').

first_reason: A bare 'burl' is often a woody swelling on a trunk or branch, not a lignotuber. It is only a lignotuber when it sits at the base or root crown.
reason: A basal burl (Vaccinium 'stem base a burl', Arctostaphylos) is a lignotuber. A burl on a trunk or branch is a woody outgrowth, not a lignotuber.

first_reason: 'Vagrant' is not a botanical term. It is probably an OCR or spelling error for 'vaginant'. Fix it as a spelling correction only after checking the source text; do not map it as a synonym.
reason: 'Vagrant lamina' turns up only in Fissidens treatments (NYBG and others: 'vagrant laminae about half the length', 'unbordered'). It is a systematic misreading of 'vaginant lamina', with no other possible meaning, so the rule works as the spelling fix.

first_reason: Same as R3518: 'vagrant laminae' is not a botanical term and is probably an error for 'vaginant laminae'.
reason: Plural of R3518; same Fissidens-only misreading of 'vaginant laminae'.

first_reason: A tooth is a shallower division than a lobe, so mapping 'tooth' to 'lobe' loses the difference. Keep this for lobes only, or use a separate tooth class.
reason: PO keeps teeth and lobes apart as separate classes (leaf lamina tooth PO_0025518 next to the lobe classes). Mapping teeth to involucre lobe would break that split, and we have no tooth class for the involucre. It needs an involucre-tooth class or a 'tooth part of involucre' pattern.

first_reason: 'Involucral tooth' is a tooth, not a lobe. See R3520.
reason: Adjective form of R3520; drop for the same reason.

first_reason: 'Leaf cells' covers every cell of the leaf, including costa, alar and marginal cells, not only the lamina. It should map to a general leaf cell class, or be mapped only when the text is clearly about the lamina.
reason: Follow R3661 'leaf cell': plant cell with container leaf (PO_0025034). 'Leaf cells' includes costal, alar and marginal cells, not only laminal cells.

first_reason: 'Male zone' is a spadix zone only in Araceae and similar plants. Apply it only when the container is a spadix.
reason: The class is part of a spadix (Araceae). 'Male zone' is also used for unisexual zones of other inflorescences and for the androecial zone of flowers. Map it only on a spadix, or on an inflorescence where the spadix is meant.

first_reason: 'Staminate zone' can refer to other inflorescences, so require a spadix container.
reason: FLOPO_0986106 is the general class and FLOPO_0986101 is its spadix subclass, as the review of the new definitions found. That review also said the general word 'staminate zone' belongs on FLOPO_0986106. Pointing the rule there is right for Araceae and for Typha, Euphorbiaceae and other spikes, and needs no spadix context.

first_reason: 'Zone mâle' is a spadix zone only in Araceae. Require a spadix container.
reason: French 'zone mâle' is the same general word as 'male zone' and 'staminate zone'. Point it to the general inflorescence class, which already covers the spadix.

first_reason: The phrase says the anthers are fused to each other, which is a quality of the anthers. It does not name the tube as a part. Mapping it to the tube drops the fusion statement and can double-count it when the text also says 'anther tube'.
reason: 'Syngenesious' says the anthers are fused into a tube. That is a quality of the anthers (connate), not the name of a part. Mapping it to anther tube loses the fusion statement. Handle it as anther plus a connate quality, by a pattern.

first_reason: The target is specific to the spadix (Araceae). A female zone also occurs in Typha spikes, catkins and other inflorescences, which are not spadices.
reason: There is no general pistillate-zone class, and the target is spadix-specific. 'Female zone' is also used for Typha, Sparganium and catkins. A pistillate zone is on the spadix, not the spathe, so require spadix only.

first_reason: Pistillate zone is also used for Typha, Sparganium and sedge inflorescences. The target class is spadix-specific.
reason: Same as R3564. The target is right only in a spadix context.

first_reason: Same as R3565: correct for a spadix, not for other inflorescences.
reason: Same as R3564.

first_reason: Staminate or male portion can also mean the male part of a flower or a plant. It maps to the target only when the whole is an inflorescence.
reason: Staminate portion of an inflorescence fits the target. Without an inflorescence context it may mean part of a flower or a plant. The spathe is not the bearer of the zone, so drop it from the list.

first_reason: Male portion is vague and can refer to a flower or a plant. It fits the target only for inflorescences.
reason: Same as R3567. 'Male portion' is vague outside an inflorescence.

first_reason: Emergence in a description means an epidermal or cortical outgrowth such as a prickle or wart. The singular is also the process of seedling emergence, which is not a part.
reason: As a part, 'emergence' means a prickle-like outgrowth from the epidermis and cortex. The singular can also mean the process of emergence, so require a bearing organ. The list adds organs that commonly carry emergences, such as the calyx or hypanthium in Rosaceae, and pedicels.

first_reason: The plural usually means outgrowths. Restrict it to organs that bear them, so the process sense is excluded.
reason: The plural 'emergences' in a description always names outgrowths, not the process. The rule fires only on a part (bearer) word, so the process sense does not arise. A list of allowed organs would only lose real cases.

first_reason: The rule drops 'adaxial'. Palms have an adaxial and an abaxial hastula, and the position is part of the meaning. Keep the position as a separate qualifier.
reason: Palms have an adaxial and an abaxial hastula, and they often differ: one present and the other absent, or of different shape. Mapping both to the same 'hastula' makes 'adaxial hastula present, abaxial absent' contradict itself. This needs subclasses or a position qualifier, not this rule.

first_reason: The rule drops 'abaxial'. The position is needed to tell the two hastulae apart.
reason: Same as R3573. Losing the position creates false contradictions.

first_reason: Pneumathode equals aerophore for the pneumatode lines on fern stipes. It also names pores on aerial roots and bark, which are a different structure.
reason: In fern descriptions, pneumathodes (lines along the stipe) are aerophores. The word is also used for pores on roots and bark, which are a different structure, so require a fern leaf part.

first_reason: A bare 'throat' also describes the calyx, the perianth or a spur. Only throat of a corolla matches the target.
reason: A bare 'throat' also belongs to the calyx (Lamiaceae), the perianth (monocots, Aristolochia) and the hypanthium. Map it to corolla throat only with a corolla context.

first_reason: Corpuscle is a general word for a small body. It means the corpusculum only in the context of the pollinarium or gynostegium.
reason: Corpuscle means the corpusculum only in Asclepiadoideae pollinaria. Elsewhere it is any small body. 'Flower' and 'corona' are too wide as context and would catch other corpuscles.

first_reason: Retinaculum is a synonym of corpusculum in Apocynaceae. In Acanthaceae it is the hooked seed support (jaculator), and in orchids it is the viscidium or stipe.
reason: Retinaculum means the corpusculum only in Apocynaceae. In Acanthaceae it is the hooked seed support, and in orchids the viscidium. A 'flower' context would let the orchid sense in, so leave it out.

first_target: corolla appendage, or a more general appendage class, not 'faucal'
first_reason: Corolla appendages include coronas, petal ligules and staminal appendages, not only those in the throat (faucal). The rule would make all of them faucal.
reason: Corolla appendages include coronas, ligules and scales outside the throat, so 'faucal' is too narrow. No existing general class for corolla appendages was found (only connective appendage and anther theca appendage). A new class is needed, not this rule.

first_reason: Bare 'propagule' also means a seed, a diaspore or a viviparous seedling (mangrove), which are not asexual propagules. Only 'vegetative propagule' is safe.
reason: Bare 'propagule' also means a fruit or seed diaspore (PO has 'propagule' as a synonym of fruit, PO_0009001) and the viviparous seedling of mangroves. It is ambiguous. The specific forms 'vegetative propagule' and 'brood body' are enough.

first_reason: Chlorophyllous cells in the sense of chlorophyllose cells belong to moss leaves. In other contexts it only means cells with chlorophyll.
reason: Chlorophyllose cells as a cell type belong to the leaves of Sphagnum and Leucobryum (and their costa). Elsewhere the phrase only describes cells with chlorophyll. Requiring a leaf context is the practical limit, since flowering-plant floras rarely use the phrase.

first_reason: Same as the singular form.
reason: Same as R3614.

first_reason: 'Green cells' is a vague phrase. It is not the specific chlorophyllose cell type.
reason: 'Green cells' is vague. It is not the specific chlorophyllose cell type of Sphagnum or Leucobryum.

first_reason: 'Dorsal wing' is used for many structures (seed, fruit, calyx, stem wings), not only the dorsal lamina.
reason: 'Dorsal wing' is used for seed, fruit, calyx and keel wings, and only sometimes for the Fissidens dorsal lamina. Even with a leaf context it is doubtful, so reject it. The rule 'dorsal lamina' covers the moss sense.

first_reason: Condyle is also an animal or generic joint term. Only an endocarp or fruit condyle matches the target.
reason: The condyle is the inward bulge of the endocarp (Menispermaceae), and the seed curves around it. Add 'seed' and 'drupe' to the context list so these common phrasings are not lost.

first_reason: 'Basal membrane' is generic (cell wall, hair, anther, ovule). The target is specific to the endostome.
reason: In moss descriptions 'basal membrane' is the standard term for the lower part of the endostome. The phrase is generic elsewhere, so require a peristome context.

first_reason: A lamella marginal cell is a cell on the lamella margin, not the lamella itself.
reason: The marginal cell of a lamella is a cell, not the lamella, so the target is wrong. Mapping it to a plain cell of the lamella would lose 'marginal', and the shape of the marginal cell (retuse, papillose, and so on) is the key Polytrichaceae character. Statements would be given to all lamella cells. This needs its own class or a pattern.

first_reason: In vascular plants 'leaf lamella' means the blade. It is a phyllid lamella only in mosses.
reason: In flora descriptions the vascular-plant blade is called 'lamina', not 'leaf lamella'. 'Leaf lamellae' is the standard Polytrichaceae and Pottiaceae term. A context constraint could not work anyway: the context words would be taxon names or 'leaf', which is already in the phrase.

first_reason: 'Basal callus' is generic. It usually means the callus of a grass floret or spikelet, or a callus on other organs, and is not the carpopodium. Use a rule only for grass parts, or reject it.
reason: In flora descriptions 'basal callus' mostly means the hardened base of a grass floret or lemma, so floret callus is the better target. The cypsela carpopodium sense is rarer. A cypsela/achene-only rule to carpopodium could be added separately.

first_reason: Calcar also names spurs on other organs (bryophyte leaves, bird or animal structures). It is a floral spur only on flower parts.
reason: Calcar is a floral spur when it is on a flower part. A spur on a short shoot is a different structure (PO short shoot has 'spur' as a synonym). Keep floral spur rather than PO petal or corolla spur, because the part bearing the spur varies.

first_reason: French éperon also means a spur on a shoot or other organs. It is a floral spur only on flower parts.
reason: French 'éperon' also means a short-shoot spur. Require a flower part, and add the French part names because this word appears in French floras.

first_reason: Lamellae are plates of cells on the leaf surface, as in Polytrichaceae. A lamella cell is not simply a cell of the costa. The container drops the lamella and may be wrong, so use no container or reject.
reason: Keep plant cell as the part, but its container should be phyllid lamella (FLOPO_0986126), which now exists, instead of costa (PO_0030072). Polytrichaceae lamellae are separate plates on the upper side of the costa, so 'cell part of costa' is not right.

target_label: plant organ apex part of perigynium
first_reason: A utricle is a perigynium only in Carex and related Cyperaceae. In Amaranthaceae and others it is a fruit. A beak is also not the same as an apex. Reject, or limit the rule to Cyperaceae.
reason: The rule's evidence is from Carex/Cyperaceae floras (17 statements in 3 floras). There, 'utricle beak' is the narrowed tip of the perigynium (PO_0009044, which has the synonym perigynia). The fruit sense of utricle is handled separately by R0457 and R1188 (PO_0030097). Fruit utricles in Amaranthaceae are rarely described with a 'beak' as a named part. Mapping a beak to the apex region (FLOPO_0985023) is the usual way to keep a named organ's beak: bare 'beak' was rejected only because it had no organ. The part-word constraint cannot pick out a family, so constraining does not help.

target_label: plant organ base part of peristome
first_reason: The peristome membrane, in mosses the basal membrane of the endostome, is a part of the peristome. It is not the base of the peristome, so the plant organ base target is wrong. Reject, or map to the peristome itself and lose the part.
reason: In moss descriptions the 'peristome membrane' is the basal membrane: the low, joined lower part of the endostome, from which the segments and cilia arise. That is a basal region of the peristome (PO_0030042), so 'plant organ base part of peristome' is a fair way to say it with existing classes. Mapping only to the peristome would lose the part. Rejecting would lose 10 statements that are clear.

first_reason: 'Capsule cell' is any cell of a capsule. Angiosperm capsules and moss capsule interior cells (spores, columella) are not exothecial cells. Use a plain plant cell, or keep the container only for the moss capsule wall.
reason: The evidence is moss capsules whose 'capsule cells' are the exothecial cells (short-rectangular, thick-walled), which is the exothecium, PO_0030073 (sporangium epidermis). Inner cells (spores, columella) have their own names and are not called 'capsule cells'. Angiosperm 'capsule 3-celled' is a count of locules carried by a quality word, not this bearer phrase. Plain plant cell would drop correct information.

target_label: native plant cell part of leaf
first_target: plant cell wall part of leaf (look up the cell wall class; do not use a cell class)
first_reason: PO_0025606 is 'native plant cell', so a wall would become a whole cell. The word names the wall of the lamina cells.
reason: The word names the wall of the leaf-blade cells, not the cell. PO has no cell-wall class; the cell wall is a GO class (GO:0005618). The previous review rejected every '... cell wall' bearer for this reason: 'basal cell wall', 'marginal cell wall', 'juxtacostal cell wall', 'inner walls'. Mapping to native plant cell (PO_0025606), or even to laminal cell (FLOPO_0986100), would turn 'walls thick, pitted' into a thick, pitted cell. Wall qualities should go through the walled-quality rules (as R1523 'lax-walled' and R1528 'thick lateral-walled' do) or wait for a decision on the cell-wall bearer.

first_target: vascular leaf part of branch (PO_0009025 with container PO_0025073)
first_reason: PO_0025075 is a leaf of a non-vascular plant, so it is correct only in bryophytes. 'Branch leaf' also occurs in conifers, lycophytes and other vascular plants.
reason: Non-vascular leaf (PO_0025075) is right only for bryophytes such as Sphagnum. 'Branch leaf' also turns up for conifers, lycophytes and other vascular plants. Leaf (PO_0025034) is the common parent of the vascular and non-vascular leaf, so it is correct in both groups and stays a part of the branch. The original rule's own note already suggests leaf for vascular floras.

target_label: plant epidermal cell part of leaf lamina adaxial epidermis
first_target: plant epidermal cell (PO_0004013) part of leaf lamina adaxial epidermis (PO_0000050)
first_reason: The target label and the container (PO_0000050, leaf lamina adaxial epidermis) are consistent. The word does not need a leaf-specific rule beyond that, because 'adaxial epidermal cell' can also be a cell of a petal or other organ. Make it a leaf-only rule or leave it to context.
reason: The target is consistent: plant epidermal cell (PO_0004013) as part of leaf lamina adaxial epidermis (PO_0000050). But that container belongs to the leaf lamina of vascular leaves. The rule's own note applies it to the moss costa as well, and adaxial epidermal cells of petals, bracts or the moss costa would be put in the wrong place. Limit it to leaf-blade contexts. Elsewhere, plain 'epidermal cell' (R3202) still applies.

first_target: phyllome lamina part of corolla (container PO_0009059)
first_reason: The corolla lamina is the limb of the whole corolla, not of one petal. A rule with petal as the whole loses the fused corolla.
reason: The examples ('laterals asymmetric', widths in mm, and R1576 'laminae not reflexing') describe the separate blades of individual petals, including the lateral ones. So lamina (PO_0025060) as part of petal (PO_0009032) fits the evidence. The fused-limb reading is not what these statements describe, and PO has no 'corolla limb' class that would be a better target.

first_reason: Kapok means the silky hairs of the capsule (Ceiba, Bombax). It is also a common name for the tree, so the rule is safe only where the bearer is a fruit, capsule or seed.
reason: As a part, kapok is the mass of silky hairs inside the capsule of Ceiba and Bombax. Trichome (PO_0000282) as part of fruit (PO_0009001) is right, and seed trichome is rightly avoided. 'Kapok' is also a common name for the tree (and a trade fibre), so the rule should fire only when the statement is about the fruit, the capsule or the seeds the hairs surround.

target_label: native plant cell part of leaf
first_reason: 'Distal' is lost. The rule sends the cells to all cells of the leaf, but moss descriptions set distal cells against basal or alar cells. A rule to a leaf-apex or distal-part container would keep that meaning. PO_0025606 (native plant cell) is also not the plant cell (PO_0009002) used by the sibling rules.
reason: Use the same cell class as the sibling rules 'leaf cell' (R3661) and 'medial laminal cells' (R3735): plant cell PO_0009002, not native plant cell PO_0025606. 'Distal' cells in moss leaves are the cells of the upper blade, which is wider than the leaf apex. So leaf apex (PO_0020137, used for 'apical laminal cell') would be too narrow. The region stays a position cue, as with the 'medial' rule. Bare 'distal cell' was rejected only because it could also mean axillary-hair cells; 'leaf distal cell' names the leaf, so the mapping is clear.

first_reason: 'Costa filament cell' is a cell of the filaments that grow on the costa surface (for example in Pottiaceae). It is not an ordinary cell of the costa. The rule loses 'filament'. Leave it unresolved or add a filament class.
reason: These are cells of the photosynthetic filaments that grow on the upper surface of the costa (Aloina, Pterygoneurum). The statements describe the filaments (cell shape, papillae, cells per filament), not ordinary costa cells. Mapping to 'plant cell part of costa' would mix the two. The previous review rejected 'filament cell' for the same missing class. There are only 2 statements, so it is better to wait for a filament class.

target_label: plant cell part of seed coat epidermis
first_reason: Seed coat cell descriptions (shape, sculpture, anticlinal walls) usually mean the epidermal cells. The rule forces the container to seed coat epidermis. It is wrong for cells of deeper layers (palisade, sclerenchyma). Keep it only when the text is about surface cells, or use seed coat as the container.
target: plant cell (PO_0009002) part of seed coat (PO_0009088)
reason: In the one source flora the statements (domed, smooth, papillate, elongate) are about the surface cells. But as a general rule, 'seed coat cell' also covers cells of deeper layers (palisade, sclereids), and seed coat epidermis (PO_0006048) would be wrong for those. The part-word constraint cannot help here because 'seed coat cell' is itself the bearer. Seed coat (PO_0009088) as the whole is always correct, and the surface reading is kept by 'testa' or 'exotesta' when the text names them.
